blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Who issues them in India, validity and extension

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.p: So the answer to "validity and extension options" on this paper is one pair of numbers, not two: six months, extendable by one month, issued by the Port Health Officer at an authorized port under the IHR. The stem confines the certificate limb to those issued to a vessel, so the seafarer's own medical certificate - which has its own authority, its own validity and its own extension rule under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 - is outside what is asked here, even though the opening sentence names the crew. Naming the crew's certificate in one line to show you know the boundary costs nothing; answering it at length spends marks the examiner has not offered.

Three questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, and the certificates in India with their validity and extension. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The last limb carries the numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO. Note what this stem does not say: it asks for the certificates "in India", without the qualifier "issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health" that other sittings of this question print - and its own first sentence names "the ship and the crew". Read plainly, the crew's medical certificate is inside the task. Answer the ship's certificates first and fully, then give the crew's its own short paragraph. That way you are complete on the wider reading and lose nothing on the narrower one.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - just two months before this paper was sat. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - TWO CLOCKS. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Two clocks, and this is the part that answers the printed words 'validity and extension options': the ship runs on six months plus one (step 5); the crew runs on two years plus three months (step 6). Same idea, different numbers, different authority.

ul: International Health Regulations (2005), as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024; the 2024 amendments in force 19 September 2025

blocks.p: The IHR content in this answer is primary-verified, read in the consolidated WHO text as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024, and the renaming of the Declaration of Health was confirmed by reading the original 2005 text alongside it rather than by inference. Two areas are weaker. The Indian administrative detail - the position of the Port Health Organisation under DGHS, the Indian Port Health Rules 1955, and the DG Shipping Statement of Compliance route for coastal trade - rests on Government and classification-society restatements rather than on the order and rules texts themselves, and is stated at that level of confidence. The list of authorized Indian ports is deliberately not reproduced: it is notified by the State Party to WHO and changes, so naming ports in a study answer would date badly. A candidate asked for specifics should say that the list is notified to and published by WHO rather than guess at it.

blocks.h: Two clocks, and why the examiner set the word "options"

blocks.p: The printed words are "validity and extension options" - plural. On this stem that plural has a real answer, because two different certificate regimes are in play and each has its own pair of numbers. The ship runs on the IHR: six months, extended by one month, and the extension exists so that a ship can reach a port where the inspection can actually be done. The crew runs on MLC Standard A1.2: two years (one if under 18, six for colour vision), extended by up to three months to the next port of call where a practitioner is available. Notice that the two extensions are built on the same idea - the document expires while the ship is somewhere the issuer is not - and that neither is a favour: both are capped, and both run to the next place the thing can be done properly. If you can set those two side by side in three lines you have answered the last limb completely, and very few candidates will.

blocks.h: Do not put DG Shipping in charge of the ship

blocks.p: This is the error that costs most marks on the India limb, and the widened certificate limb on this paper makes it easier to fall into, because both authorities now appear in the same answer. Keep them apart: the Port Health Officer, under the Port Health Organisation, DGHS and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, certifies the ship - SSCC and SSCEC, under the IHR and the Indian Port Health Rules 1955. DG Shipping, under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, approves the medical examiners who certify the seafarer. Health ministry for the hull; shipping administration for the man. Write that sentence and the limb is safe.

blocks.h: What this sitting does NOT ask, and why that is worth knowing

blocks.p: The November 2025 paper set this question in a shorter form - it asked for "the different certificates in India" with no qualifier. That omission widened the task: with nothing confining the certificates to the ship, and with the opening sentence naming the ship and the crew, the seafarer's medical certificate under MLC 2006 Regulation 1.2 and Standard A1.2 fell inside the printed demand and had to be answered - two years' validity, one year under 18, six years for colour vision, and a certificate expiring at sea continuing to the next port for not more than three months. This paper puts the qualifier back: certificates issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health. That single phrase moves the crew's certificate out of the task. Learn both, because the two sittings are one month apart and the difference between them is a phrase rather than a topic - and the skill being tested is reading the stem, not reciting the subject. The safe technique is a single sentence acknowledging that the crew hold their own certificate under a different instrument and a different authority, then spending the marks where the stem points.

questions.understand_first: There are two health systems on a ship and the question runs across both. One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. The other protects the crew, and that is labour and training law administered by the shipping administration. Keeping those two apart is what makes the India limb straightforward: the Port Health Officer certifies the ship, DG Shipping certifies the seafarer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long are ship sanitation certificates valid, and what extension is available?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of six months, for both the SSCC and the SSCEC. Extendable by one month where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at the port. IHR Article 39(1).
retrieval_cards.why: The single most examined fact in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SSCC from the SSCEC.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Exemption Certificate is issued where the authority is satisfied the ship is free of infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs, so no measures are needed. The Control Certificate is issued where measures were required and satisfactorily completed, and records the evidence found and the measures taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Exemption means nothing was needed; Control means something was done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is Article 37 called now, and what was it called before?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Ship Declaration of Health, to the model in Annex 8. In the original 2005 text it was the Maritime Declaration of Health. The change came with the amendments in force from 19 September 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Most textbooks and coaching notes still use the old name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are these still called Deratting Certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates of the earlier Regulations were replaced under the IHR 2005 by the SSCC and SSCEC, widening the scope from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who issues ship sanitation certificates in India?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO. The Port Health Organisation sits under the Directorate General of Health Services, within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and works under the Indian Port Health Rules 1955 with the IHR 2005.
retrieval_cards.why: Not DG Shipping - that side handles seafarer medical fitness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise WHO's role in four verbs.
retrieval_cards.answer: It prescribes (the Regulations and the Annex 3 and 8 models), publishes (areas where vector control is recommended, and lists of authorized ports), advises (methods and materials for disinsection and deratting) and certifies (ports, on the State Party's request, under Article 20(4)).
retrieval_cards.why: WHO does not enforce - the competent authority at the point of entry does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What distance does Annex 5 set for vector control programmes at points of entry?
retrieval_cards.answer: A minimum of 400 metres from those areas of point of entry facilities used for operations involving travellers, conveyances, containers, cargo and postal parcels - extended where vectors of greater range are present.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise, checkable figure that shows the Annex has been read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When should the sanitation inspection be carried out?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and in the case of a ship in ballast, before loading. IHR Article 39(4).
retrieval_cards.why: A printed requirement candidates routinely miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: No valid certificate is produced on arrival - what may the State Party do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Proceed under Article 27(1): treat the conveyance as affected and disinfect, decontaminate, disinsect or derat it, or have that done under its supervision, with isolation or quarantine if necessary.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 39(2) makes the cross-reference explicit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian authority certifies the ship's health, and which certifies the seafarer's?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ship: the Port Health Officer, in the Port Health Organisation under the Directorate General of Health Services and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, issuing the SSCC or SSCEC under the IHR 2005 and the Indian Port Health Rules 1955. The seafarer: a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, which acts under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, issuing the medical fitness certificate under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 and STCW.
retrieval_cards.why: Health ministry for the hull, shipping administration for the man. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates.

blocks.h: 1. The framework these processes sit inside

blocks.p: A ship using LNG as fuel is designed and operated under SOLAS chapter II-1 part G and the IGF Code; the bunkering operation itself is specified by ISO 20519 - equipment, procedures, competence and documentation. Safety rests on a two-stage emergency shutdown system, with the delivery facility and the receiving ship joined by an ESD link so both act together. Before transfer, a safety zone is set, compatibility and mooring agreed, and the checklist and bunkering plan completed.

Carried out when a tank is being brought back into service after refit, repair or inerting - before any liquid is introduced. The tank is full of inert gas or nitrogen, and that atmosphere must be replaced with methane vapour.

ul: Why. Any carbon dioxide in inert gas would freeze at LNG temperature and block valves, filters and lines. Nitrogen does not freeze but is non-condensable: it accumulates in the vapour space, raises tank pressure, degrades the fuel's calorific value and upsets reliquefaction and gas supply.

How. LNG is taken from the supply through a vaporiser to produce warm methane vapour, which is admitted at the top of the tank. Being lighter than nitrogen, it forms a layer that pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line.
Where it goes. The displaced gas is led to the vent mast with attention to dispersion, or returned to the supply.

Completion. Sampling at the outlet continues until the hydrocarbon content reaches the specified value and carbon dioxide falls below its limit. The figures are set by the ship's manual and the containment system, not by a universal rule.

blocks.p: Once the tank holds methane vapour it is still warm. Cooling down brings the tank, pipework and manifold gradually towards LNG temperature, about minus 162 degrees Celsius, before bulk filling begins.

ul: Why. To avoid thermal shock and excessive thermal stress in the tank structure and insulation; and to avoid the violent flash-off that occurs when LNG meets warm surfaces, which would over-pressurise the tank and swamp the vapour handling capacity.
How. LNG is admitted in small controlled quantities through spray nozzles at the top of the tank, evaporating as it falls and cooling the structure evenly.

Rate control. The permitted rate of temperature fall is limited by the tank designer and class, and temperatures are watched at fixed sensors through the tank to keep the structure cooling uniformly rather than locally.
Completion. When the sensors reach the target and are stable, bulk transfer starts at a low initial rate and is ramped up only once pressures and temperatures are seen to be steady.

blocks.p: LNG boils continuously from heat ingress, and filling a tank displaces the vapour already in it. Vapour management is the control of tank pressure within the design limit throughout, and it is the process that actually governs how fast bunkering can proceed.

ul: Vapour return line - the primary method. A connection back to the bunker source returns the displaced vapour to its tanks, balancing pressure on both sides and removing the need to vent to atmosphere.
Consumption - burning the gas in the ship's engines, boilers or generators where the plant is running.
Reliquefaction where fitted, returning boil-off to the tank as liquid.
Gas combustion unit - burning off surplus gas safely where it cannot be used.
Controlled venting to the vent mast - a last resort only, because released methane is a potent greenhouse gas and venting is operationally and environmentally constrained.

Supporting controls. Spray filling to condense vapour; monitoring against the relief valve setting; level alarms and ESD trips; and attention to stratification and rollover where LNG of a different density is loaded onto an existing heel.

blocks.p: The emergency release system exists so that the transfer connection can be parted quickly and without spilling if the two vessels move beyond safe limits, if moorings fail, or in fire. Its heart is the emergency release coupling - a dry-break coupling with interlocked isolating valves which close before the halves separate, so the liquid held in the line is contained and the release of LNG and gas is minimised.

ul: ESD-1 - stop the pumps and close the manifold valves on both sides. Transfer ceases. Triggered manually from either end or automatically by tank level, pressure, gas detection or fire.
Drain and reduce inventory in the transfer line so far as the time available allows.

ESD-2 - the release stage. The coupling's isolating valves close first, then the coupling parts at its designed point. Initiation is manual, or automatic from mooring load or vessel position monitoring exceeding its limits.
After release - both sides are purged with nitrogen, the parted hose end is made safe, and personnel stay clear of the release zone while residual liquid boils off.

Before transfer the ESD link must be connected and function-tested, the coupling confirmed armed and certified, communications and agreed emergency signals established, and the release covered in the bunkering plan and drilled.

blocks.p: Four processes are named, so the examiner is marking four visible blocks. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write one long essay on LNG bunkering and leave the marker hunting for the four headings. Head each one exactly as printed. One short framing paragraph first is worth having - it lets you name the IGF Code, ISO 20519 and the ESD link once, so all four processes can then refer back to them without repetition.

blocks.h: The idea that ties the four together

blocks.p: Three of the four are about vapour and temperature, not liquid. That is the whole point. In LNG work the danger is rarely the liquid sitting in a tank - it is the gas you create by doing something too fast. Gassing up removes an atmosphere that would freeze or accumulate; cooling down prevents the flash-off that a warm tank would produce; vapour management disposes of the gas that filling inevitably generates. The emergency release is the fourth because it accepts that despite all of that, the connection may still have to be broken - and even then the design goal is the same, to part the line without releasing what is inside it. The order is also the order of the operation: you cannot cool a tank you have not gassed up, and you cannot fill one you have not cooled.

blocks.h: Why gassing up comes before cooling down

blocks.p: Because the freezing problem has to be solved while everything is still warm. Inert gas from a generator carries carbon dioxide, which becomes a solid well above LNG temperature. Introduce liquid into a tank that still holds carbon dioxide and you produce dry ice inside valves, strainers and spray lines - exactly where you least want a blockage. Gassing up removes it first. Nitrogen is a gentler problem but a persistent one: it will not freeze, but because it does not condense it stays in the vapour space, builds pressure, and thins the gas going to the engines. So gassing up is not a formality before the real work; it is what makes the cooling stage survivable.

ul: Reversing the order - cooling down before gassing up. Liquid must not enter a tank still holding inert gas.
Saying gassing up removes air. Air was removed earlier by inerting; gassing up removes the inert gas or nitrogen and replaces it with methane vapour.
Describing cooling down as "filling slowly". It is spray cooling through nozzles at a controlled rate of temperature fall, not a slow bulk fill.
Treating venting as normal vapour management. It is a last resort; the vapour return line is the primary route and methane venting carries a real environmental penalty.
Describing the emergency release coupling as a hose that simply breaks. Its defining feature is the interlocked isolating valves that close before separation.
Conflating ESD-1 and ESD-2. Stopping the transfer and parting the connection are two different stages, and ESD-2 follows ESD-1.

blocks.p:
"Why not use inert gas from the generator and go straight to loading?" Carbon dioxide in the inert gas freezes at LNG temperature and blocks the system. That single sentence is what the gassing-up limb is really testing.

"What limits how fast you can bunker?" Not the pump - the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. Bunkering is paced by where the gas can go.

"The bunker vessel starts to drift. What happens first?" ESD-1 stops the transfer and closes the manifold valves; only then does ESD-2 operate the release coupling. Going straight to "the hose disconnects" misses the sequence.

"You loaded a different LNG on top of your heel. What is the risk?" Stratification and rollover - a sudden mixing of layers of different density releasing a large volume of vapour and spiking tank pressure.

ul: What is the purpose of gassing up? To displace inert gas or nitrogen with methane vapour before liquid is admitted, chiefly to remove carbon dioxide that would freeze.
Why is warm vapour admitted at the top of the tank? It is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier gas out through the bottom line.
What is the approximate temperature of LNG? About minus 162 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure.
What is the primary route for displaced vapour during bunkering? The vapour return line back to the bunkering facility.
What does an emergency release coupling do that an ordinary quick-release does not? Its interlocked isolating valves close before the coupling parts, containing the line inventory.
What links the two ESD systems? A ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link, so that shutdown on either side acts on both.

blocks.p: CLEAN - CHILL - CONTROL - CUT. Clean the atmosphere (step 2, gassing up). Chill the structure (step 3, cooling down). Control the pressure (step 4, vapour management). Cut the connection safely if it all goes wrong (step 5, emergency release). Step 1 is the framework they all sit in. The four Cs run in the same order as the operation itself.

ul: SOLAS chapter II-1 part G and the IGF Code (resolution MSC.391(95)) - design, arrangement and operation of ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels
ISO 20519 - Specification for bunkering of liquefied natural gas fuelled vessels: equipment, procedures, competence, documentation and the LNG bunker delivery note
ISO 20519 - the emergency release system shall consist of an emergency release coupling including interlocked isolating valves to minimize loss of LNG or natural gas on activation
ISO 20519 - the delivery facility and receiving vessel ESD systems shall be interconnected by a ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore ESD link for coordinated operation

Ship-specific documents: the containment system manual, the bunkering plan and the ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore checklist, which set the actual completion criteria and rates

blocks.p: The emergency release architecture and the vapour return function are primary-verified against ISO 20519 - the interlocked isolating valves within the coupling, and the interconnected ESD link, are that standard's own requirements. Two areas are weaker and are stated at their real strength. MIW holds no licensed copy of the IGF Code, so the framework statements rest on IMO and classification-society material rather than on the code text. And the numbers deliberately are not fixed: the hydrocarbon and carbon dioxide percentages that end gassing up, and the permitted rate of temperature fall during cooldown, are set by the containment system designer, the class rules and the ship's own manual, and vary between membrane and independent tank types. They are described as parameters to be read off the ship's documents rather than reduced to a single figure that would be wrong on most ships. ISO 20519 also exists in more than one edition; the requirements used here are those consistent across editions, and no clause numbers are cited. Finally, the ESD-1 then ESD-2 ordering is presented as the standard arrangement, because the precise trigger logic is set by the equipment maker's design and by the agreed bunkering plan.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: One connection is worth carrying away, and it is the reason this question rewards understanding over memorised procedure. Everything in limbs (a) to (c) exists to control the rate at which gas is generated and disposed of: the bunkering operation is paced by vapour, not by liquid. The same logic governs a gas-fuelled main engine in service. A fouled hull or a heavy sea drives the engine into the torque-rich region, where it demands more fuel at a lower speed - and on a gas engine that demand runs straight into the fuel-gas supply system's pressure and temperature limits, with knock and misfire as the symptoms rather than exhaust temperature and smoke. In both cases the fuel system, not the fuel tank, is the constraint. Being able to say that in one sentence is the difference between two memorised procedures and an understanding of gas-fuelled operation. If you want to see the propulsion side of the same point worked through, it is set out at QP2511 Q2, the propeller-curve question on the November 2025 paper.

EMERGENCY RELEASE - ESD-1 stops pumps and closes manifold valves; ESD-2 then closes the coupling's INTERLOCKED ISOLATING VALVES BEFORE the halves part, so the line inventory is contained; purge with nitrogen and secure the parted end. The ESD link must be function-tested before transfer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a tank be gassed up before LNG is admitted?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because carbon dioxide in inert gas freezes solid at LNG temperature and would block valves, strainers and spray lines; and nitrogen, while it will not freeze, is non-condensable, so it accumulates in the vapour space, raises pressure and thins the gas supplied to the engines.
retrieval_cards.why: The freezing point is what the limb is really testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is gassing up carried out, and why at the top of the tank?
retrieval_cards.answer: LNG is passed through a vaporiser to give warm methane vapour, admitted at the top of the tank. Methane vapour is lighter than nitrogen, so it layers above and pushes the heavier inert gas down and out through the bottom liquid line to the vent mast or back to the supply.
retrieval_cards.why: Density difference is what makes the displacement work.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is cooling down for, and how is it done?
retrieval_cards.answer: To bring tank, pipework and manifold gradually to about minus 162 degrees Celsius, avoiding thermal shock to the structure and the violent flash-off that LNG produces on warm surfaces. Done by spraying small controlled quantities of LNG through nozzles at the top, within the rate of temperature fall set by the designer and class.
retrieval_cards.why: Spray cooling at a controlled rate, not a slow bulk fill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Rank the routes for vapour during bunkering.
retrieval_cards.answer: Vapour return line to the bunker source first; then consumption in engines, boilers or generators; then reliquefaction where fitted; then a gas combustion unit for surplus. Controlled venting to the vent mast is a last resort only, because methane is a potent greenhouse gas.
retrieval_cards.why: Venting last is the point - it is not routine practice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes an emergency release coupling different from an ordinary quick-release?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its interlocked isolating valves close before the two halves separate, so the liquid held in the transfer line is contained and the loss of LNG or natural gas on activation is minimised.
retrieval_cards.why: The valves, not the parting, are the safety feature.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the emergency release sequence.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESD-1 stops the pumps and closes the manifold valves on both sides, ending transfer. Line inventory is drained as far as time allows. ESD-2 then closes the coupling's isolating valves and the coupling parts. Both sides purge with nitrogen and the parted end is secured.
retrieval_cards.why: Two stages, in order - stop first, part second.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What actually limits the rate at which a ship can be bunkered with LNG?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not the pump, but the vapour handling capacity and the tank pressure limit. The rate is paced by where the displaced and boil-off gas can go - principally the vapour return line - and by keeping pressure below the relief valve setting.
retrieval_cards.why: Bunkering speed is a vapour problem, not a liquid one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instruments govern LNG-fuelled ships and their bunkering?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS chapter II-1 part G with the IGF Code (resolution MSC.391(95)) for the ship's design, arrangement and operation; ISO 20519 for the bunkering operation, covering equipment, procedures, competence and the LNG bunker delivery note.
retrieval_cards.why: One for the ship, one for the transfer.

blocks.h: 1. The statute these principles come from

blocks.p: For an Indian examination the governing statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It codifies the law of marine insurance in India and follows the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 closely - the 1906 Act may be named as the source it follows, but it must not be cited in its place, and the later English reforms of insurance law do not apply in India. Section 3 gives the contract itself: a contract of marine insurance is an agreement whereby the insurer undertakes to indemnify the assured, in the manner and to the extent thereby agreed, against marine losses.

The principles below are not decoration. Marine insurance is a promise to pay for something that has not happened yet, made by someone who cannot inspect the ship, about a voyage he cannot watch. Each principle answers one way that arrangement could be abused.

The rule. Section 7 - every person has an insurable interest who is interested in a marine adventure; in particular, a person is so interested where he stands in any legal or equitable relation to the adventure or to any insurable property at risk, such that he may benefit by its safety or due arrival, may be prejudiced by its loss or damage or detention, or may incur liability in respect of it. Section 8 fixes the timing: the assured must be interested at the time of the loss, though he need not be when the insurance is effected - and where the subject-matter is insured "lost or not lost" he may recover even if he acquired his interest after the loss, unless he knew of the loss and the insurer did not. Section 6 supplies the sanction: a contract of marine insurance by way of wagering is void, including a policy made "interest or no interest".

Example. A shipowner has an insurable interest in his ship, and a cargo owner in his cargo. A charterer has an interest in the hire he stands to lose and in liabilities he may incur. But a Chief Engineer has no insurable interest in the ship he serves on - he is prejudiced by her loss only in employment, not in property - so a policy he took out on her hull would be a wager and void under section 6. Conversely, if cargo is sold afloat and the risk passes to the buyer, the buyer acquires the interest and can recover, even for a loss that occurred before he bought, under a "lost or not lost" policy.

The rule. Section 19 - a contract of marine insurance is a contract based upon the utmost good faith, and if it is not observed by either party the other may avoid the contract. It is mutual, and it operates before the contract is concluded. Section 20 - the assured must disclose to the insurer, before the contract is concluded, every material circumstance known to him, and he is deemed to know every circumstance which in the ordinary course of business ought to be known by him. A circumstance is material if it would influence the judgement of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether to take the risk. In the absence of enquiry, need not be disclosed: circumstances diminishing the risk; matters known or presumed known to the insurer; matters he has waived; and matters covered by an express or implied warranty. Sections 21 and 22 extend the duty to the assured's agent and to representations during negotiation.

Example. The vessel is fixed to load in a port where she has already suffered heavy weather damage to her hatch covers, or the owner knows the main engine has an unrepaired crankshaft defect. Both are material and must be disclosed. Failing to do so entitles the insurer to avoid the policy from the outset - and note the consequence, because it is what makes the principle bite: the contract is voidable, not void, the avoidance operates ab initio, and non-disclosure need not be fraudulent. An honest oversight has the same effect as concealment.

The rule. From section 3 - the insurer undertakes to indemnify. The assured is to be placed, so far as money can, in the position he occupied immediately before the loss - and no better. Marine insurance is a contract of indemnity and not one of profit. Two sections show it working: section 81, where the assured is insured for less than the insurable value, he is deemed his own insurer for the balance; and the measure-of-indemnity provisions, which fix what is actually recoverable rather than what was lost emotionally.

Example. A twenty-year-old auxiliary engine is destroyed by an insured peril and replaced with a new one. The assured recovers the value of what he lost, not the price of a new machine - the betterment is his. Similarly, a ship insured for one crore whose insurable value is two crore recovers only half of a partial loss, because under section 81 she is self-insured for the other half. Marine insurance is a qualified indemnity in practice, because a valued policy agrees the value in advance and that agreed value is conclusive between the parties - which is worth saying, as it is the one place where the principle is deliberately relaxed.

The rule. Section 79 - where the insurer pays for a total loss of the whole, or of an apportionable part of goods, he becomes entitled to take over the interest of the assured in whatever remains of the subject-matter paid for, and is subrogated to all the rights and remedies of the assured in respect of it as from the time of the casualty causing the loss. Where he pays for a partial loss he acquires no title to the subject-matter but is still subrogated to the assured's rights and remedies. Subrogation is the corollary of indemnity: it stops the assured recovering twice for one loss, once from the insurer and once from the wrongdoer.

Example. The ship is damaged in a collision for which the other vessel is wholly to blame. The hull underwriters pay the repair cost, and step into the owner's shoes to pursue the other vessel's owners for that sum - in the owner's name. It follows that the assured must not prejudice those rights: signing away a claim against a stevedore who damaged the cargo, or a repairer who caused the failure, may cost the assured the indemnity itself.

The rule. Section 80 - where the assured is over-insured by double insurance, each insurer is bound, as between himself and the others, to contribute rateably to the loss in proportion to the amount for which he is liable under his own contract; and an insurer who pays more than his proportion may sue the others for contribution, with the remedies of a surety who has overpaid. Contribution is again the servant of indemnity - the assured may claim in full from one insurer, but he cannot collect the same loss twice, and the insurers settle the sharing among themselves.

Example. A cargo is insured by the seller under an open cover and again by the buyer under his own policy, both policies attaching to the same interest for the same voyage. On a claim the assured need not chase both; he recovers from one, and that insurer recovers a rateable proportion from the other under section 80. If the two policies total more than the insurable value, the assured still recovers only the value of the loss.

The rule. Section 55 - the insurer is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against, and is not liable for any loss which is not so proximately caused. Proximate means the dominant or effective cause, not the one nearest in time. Section 55 then names exclusions which stand unless the policy provides otherwise, and two are worth carrying: the insurer is not liable for loss attributable to the wilful misconduct of the assured, but is liable for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril even though it would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew.

Example. A ship strands because the officer of the watch made a navigational error. The proximate cause is stranding, an insured peril, and the negligence of the crew does not defeat the claim - section 55 says so expressly. But if the owner himself sent her to sea knowing she was unfit and she is lost in consequence, the dominant cause is his own conduct and the claim fails. That second half is where this principle meets seaworthiness, and it is the reason the two topics are so often examined together.

blocks.h: 8. Mitigation - the duty to sue and labour

blocks.p: The rule. Insurance does not licence the assured to stand and watch. Where the policy contains a suing and labouring clause, section 78 makes the engagement supplementary to the contract of insurance, and the assured may recover from the insurer the expenses properly incurred under it - notwithstanding that the insurer may have paid for a total loss, or that the subject-matter was warranted free from particular average. The assured and his agents are expected to take reasonable measures to avert or minimise a loss.

Example. After a flooding in the engine room, the Chief Engineer runs the emergency bilge suction, arranges shore pumps and lands the damaged spares for cleaning and preservation. Those costs are recoverable as sue and labour, in addition to the claim itself. Doing nothing, and allowing salt water to write off machinery that could have been saved, risks the insurer declining that part of the loss.

The command is discuss, then explain each of the principle with suitable examples. Two things follow. First, every principle must carry an example - a list of principles without examples answers only half the question, and it is the half worth fewer marks because the examples are what show understanding. Second, the number of principles is left to the candidate, so choose a defensible set and head each one. Six is the classical set - insurable interest, utmost good faith, indemnity, subrogation, contribution, proximate cause. Mitigation is a legitimate seventh and is worth adding because it is the one an engineer can speak about from experience. Do not exceed that: a thin list of nine beats nothing.

blocks.h: Anchor every principle to a section

blocks.p: This is what separates a Class I answer from a general-knowledge one. Every principle here has a section of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 behind it - 7 and 8, 19 and 20, 3 and 81, 79, 80, 55, 78 - and quoting the section costs one line and gains disproportionately. Equally important is which Act: for an Indian paper it is the 1963 Act. The English Marine Insurance Act 1906 is the model it follows and may be named as such; citing the 1906 Act instead is a jurisdiction error, and citing later English insurance-law reform is worse, because that reform does not apply in India at all.

blocks.h: The idea that ties them together

blocks.p: Five of the seven exist to enforce one idea: insurance restores, it does not enrich. Indemnity states it. Insurable interest ensures there is a real loss to restore, and not a bet. Subrogation stops the assured recovering the same loss twice, from insurer and wrongdoer. Contribution stops him recovering it twice from two insurers. Mitigation stops him letting the loss grow because someone else is paying. The remaining two protect the bargain itself: utmost good faith ensures the insurer priced the risk he actually took, and proximate cause ensures he pays only for the risk he agreed to carry. Say that in two sentences before the list, and the seven headings stop reading as memorised vocabulary.

ul: Citing the English MIA 1906 for an Indian paper. The 1963 Act governs. Name 1906 only as the model.
Listing the principles and omitting the examples. The stem asks for examples expressly.
Saying insurable interest must exist when the policy is taken out. Section 8 requires it at the time of the loss; it need not exist at inception.
Saying non-disclosure makes the contract void. It is voidable at the insurer's option, avoided ab initio.
Saying the non-disclosure must be fraudulent. It need not be - an innocent failure to disclose a material circumstance is enough.
Treating proximate cause as the last or nearest in time cause. It is the dominant and effective cause.

Saying crew negligence defeats a claim. Section 55 says the opposite - the insurer is liable for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril even though it would not have happened but for the negligence of master or crew.
Confusing subrogation (insurer recovers from the wrongdoer) with contribution (insurer recovers a share from another insurer).
Omitting the effect of under-insurance under section 81 - the assured is his own insurer for the balance.

blocks.p: "You are Chief Engineer. Can you insure the ship?" No - no insurable interest in the hull, so the policy would be a wager and void under section 6. You can insure your own effects and your liability. "Cargo was already lost when the buyer bought it. Can he claim?" Under a "lost or not lost" policy, yes - unless he knew of the loss and the insurer did not (section 8). "The Second Engineer's error caused the flooding. Does the claim fail?" No - section 55(2)(a) preserves the claim for a loss proximately caused by an insured peril notwithstanding the negligence of master or crew. "The owner knew she was unseaworthy and sent her anyway." Different answer - that is the assured's own conduct, and it defeats the claim. "The engine was twenty years old and you got a new one." You recover the value lost, not the betterment - indemnity, not profit.

ul: Which Act governs marine insurance in India? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Define insurable interest. Section 7 - a legal or equitable relation to the adventure or the property at risk, such that you benefit by its safety or are prejudiced by its loss.
When must the interest exist? At the time of the loss - section 8.
What is uberrimae fidei? Section 19 - utmost good faith, mutual, and breach lets the other party avoid the contract.
What need not be disclosed? Section 20 - circumstances diminishing the risk, matters known or presumed known to the insurer, matters waived, and matters covered by a warranty.
What is subrogation? Section 79 - on payment the insurer takes over the assured's rights and remedies against third parties.
What is contribution? Section 80 - rateable sharing between insurers where the assured is over-insured by double insurance.
State the rule of proximate cause. Section 55 - the insurer is liable for loss proximately caused by an insured peril and not otherwise.
What is sue and labour? Section 78 - expenses properly incurred to avert or minimise a loss are recoverable in addition, even if a total loss is paid.

blocks.p: I - U - I - S - C - P - M. Insurable interest (2), Utmost good faith (3), Indemnity (4), Subrogation (5), Contribution (6), Proximate cause (7), Mitigation (8). Sections in the same order: 7 and 8, 19 and 20, 3 and 81, 79, 80, 55, 78. Five of the seven serve indemnity; two protect the bargain.

ul: Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India), section 3 - marine insurance defined; the undertaking to indemnify.
Section 6 - avoidance of wagering contracts; 'interest or no interest' policies void.
Sections 7 and 8 - insurable interest defined; when interest must attach; 'lost or not lost'.
Section 19 - insurance is uberrimae fidei. Section 20 - disclosure by the assured, materiality, and what need not be disclosed. Sections 21 and 22 - disclosure by an agent; representations.
Section 55 - included and excluded losses; proximate cause; wilful misconduct of the assured; negligence of master or crew.
Section 78 - suing and labouring clause.
Section 79 - right of subrogation, total and partial loss.
Section 80 - right of contribution on double insurance. Section 81 - effect of under-insurance.
Sections 35 to 43 - warranties, including the implied warranty of seaworthiness in a voyage policy - the doctrine that sits alongside these principles and is examined with them.
Section 66 - general average loss. English Marine Insurance Act 1906 - the model the 1963 Act follows; named, never substituted.

blocks.p: Jurisdiction is the live risk on this question, not currency. The principles of marine insurance are stable and have not moved; what moves is which statute a candidate cites. For an Indian paper the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is the operative statute and every section above is a section of it, read in the Act's own text. The English Marine Insurance Act 1906 is the model and may be named as such. Later English reform of insurance law - which changed the consequences of non-disclosure in England - does not apply in India, and the section 19 and 20 position stated above is the Indian one.

Provenance of the text. The Act's sections were read in a full text of the 1963 Act, and the copy used was checked against sections this corpus had already verified independently through earlier papers - sections 2, 19, 20 and 66 - before the unverified sections were relied on. MIW holds no certified consolidated print, so no claim is made about the amendment history of any individual section.

What is not asserted. No case law is cited. The principles are stated from the statute, and the illustrative examples are worked applications of the sections rather than reports of decided cases - no example above should be read as a case authority. Market practice on valued policies, deductibles and Institute Clauses is named where it qualifies a statutory rule but is not detailed, because the stem asks for the principles and the clauses are not part of the Act.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q8 on this paper. Section 55 of the Marine Insurance Act preserves a claim despite the negligence of master or crew, but not despite the assured's own conduct - and unseaworthiness is the classic instance of that conduct. Q8 asks what an unseaworthy ship is under the Merchant Shipping Act, which is a criminal question; here the same fact pattern is a recovery question. One ship, one defect, two entirely different consequences depending on which statute is asking. That contrast is worth carrying into the exam, because examiners set the pair deliberately.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the principles of marine insurance and their sections in the Indian Act.
retrieval_cards.answer: Insurable interest, sections 7 and 8. Utmost good faith, sections 19 and 20. Indemnity, section 3 with section 81. Subrogation, section 79. Contribution, section 80. Proximate cause, section 55. Mitigation or sue and labour, section 78. All Marine Insurance Act 1963.
retrieval_cards.why: The section numbers are what lift this answer above general knowledge.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Marine Insurance Act applies on an Indian paper?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It codifies marine insurance law in India and follows the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 closely, so 1906 may be named as the model it follows, but must never be cited in its place. Later English reform of insurance law does not apply in India.
retrieval_cards.why: A jurisdiction error that costs marks on an otherwise correct answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When must insurable interest exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 8. At the time of the loss, though not necessarily when the insurance is effected. Where the subject-matter is insured 'lost or not lost' the assured may recover even though he acquired his interest after the loss, unless at the time of contracting he knew of the loss and the insurer did not. Under section 8(2) he cannot acquire an interest by any act or election after he is aware of the loss.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest error is to say the interest must exist at inception.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a material circumstance, and what need not be disclosed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 20. A circumstance is material if it would influence the judgement of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether to take the risk. In the absence of enquiry, the assured need not disclose circumstances which diminish the risk, matters known or presumed known to the insurer, matters the insurer has waived, and matters covered by an express or implied warranty.
retrieval_cards.why: The four exceptions are a standing question and are easily half-remembered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does non-disclosure make the policy void, and must it be fraudulent?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither. Under section 19 the innocent party may avoid the contract, so it is voidable at the insurer's option rather than void, and the avoidance operates ab initio. The non-disclosure need not be fraudulent - an honest failure to disclose a material circumstance is enough to found avoidance.
retrieval_cards.why: Two precise points that candidates routinely get the wrong way round.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish subrogation from contribution.
retrieval_cards.answer: Subrogation, section 79, is the insurer stepping into the assured's shoes to pursue a third party who caused the loss, after paying the claim. Contribution, section 80, is between insurers - where the assured is over-insured by double insurance, each contributes rateably in proportion to his own liability, and an insurer who pays more than his share may sue the others. Both exist to stop the assured recovering the same loss twice.
retrieval_cards.why: The pair is examined together precisely because they are confused.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the crew's negligence defeat a hull claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 55(2)(a) provides that the insurer is not liable for loss attributable to the wilful misconduct of the assured, but, unless the policy otherwise provides, he is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against even though the loss would not have happened but for the misconduct or negligence of the master or crew. The assured's own conduct is a different matter and does defeat the claim.
retrieval_cards.why: The section says the opposite of what candidates assume.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the rule of proximate cause and what 'proximate' means.
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 55(1). Subject to the Act and unless the policy otherwise provides, the insurer is liable for any loss proximately caused by a peril insured against, and is not liable for any loss which is not proximately caused by a peril insured against. Proximate means the dominant and effective cause of the loss, not the cause nearest in time.
retrieval_cards.why: The time-based misreading is the classic error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is sue and labour, and can you recover it on top of a total loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 78. Where the policy contains a suing and labouring clause, the engagement is supplementary to the contract of insurance and the assured may recover from the insurer expenses properly incurred under it - notwithstanding that the insurer may have paid for a total loss, or that the subject-matter was warranted free from particular average. So yes, it is recoverable in addition.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'notwithstanding a total loss' point is the part worth the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the effect of under-insurance?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 81. Where the assured is insured for less than the insurable value, or in the case of a valued policy for less than the policy valuation, he is deemed to be his own insurer in respect of the uninsured balance, and bears that proportion of any loss himself.
retrieval_cards.why: The practical face of indemnity, and the arithmetic examiners like to set.

blocks.h: 1. What Maslow proposed, and what kind of authority it is

blocks.p: Abraham Maslow set out his theory in A Theory of Human Motivation (1943) and developed it in Motivation and Personality (1954). It is management and psychological literature, not a regulatory requirement - no convention prescribes a theory of motivation, and it should be attributed as what it is. Its claim is that human needs are hierarchical: they arrange themselves in an order of prepotency, so that a lower, unsatisfied need dominates behaviour until it is relatively satisfied, whereupon the next level emerges as the motivator.

Two consequences follow, and they are the whole practical value of the theory: a satisfied need is no longer a motivator, and you cannot motivate at a level above the one a person is actually stuck on. Offering recognition to a man who has not slept properly for a fortnight, or career development to one who has not been paid, does not work - and Maslow explains why.

blocks.h: 2. The five levels, read onto a ship

ol: Physiological - food, water, sleep, warmth. On board: adequate rest and hours of rest actually observed, edible and sufficient food, drinking water, a cabin cool enough and quiet enough to sleep in, sanitary facilities that work. This is the level a ship most often fails at, and it is the level that disables every other one.

Safety and security - freedom from danger and from uncertainty. On board: a safe engine room, working PPE, enforced permit-to-work and enclosed-space procedures, machinery guards, but equally job security, wages paid on time, a contract that ends when it says it does, and a credible expectation of relief and repatriation on the due date.

Social - love and belonging. On board: acceptance in the engine-room team and in the ship's company, being spoken to rather than about, contact with family - which today means workable connectivity - a mess where mixed nationalities are not segregated, and recreation.

Esteem - recognition, status, competence, respect from others and self-respect. On board: credit given by name for a job done well, responsibility entrusted, being consulted on the work one performs, rank and role respected, appraisals that are honest and useful rather than a formality.

Self-actualisation - realising one's full potential. On board: promotion and the training that leads to it, a genuinely challenging job, being given charge of a project, mentoring juniors, and support for certificates of competency.

blocks.h: 3. What the theory claims, and where it is weak

blocks.p: The mechanism is prepotency plus relative satisfaction - Maslow did not claim a level must be completely satisfied before the next appears, and he allowed movement back down when a lower need is threatened. A man secure and well regarded on Monday can be driven straight back to the safety level on Tuesday by news that the company is not paying wages.

The honest limitations are worth a sentence, because a Chief Engineer applying the theory needs them. The empirical support for a strict five-level ordering is weak; the ordering is culturally variable, and a multinational crew will not rank belonging and esteem identically; the levels overlap rather than queue; and Maslow himself never drew the pyramid the diagram is always given as. Later models - notably Alderfer's compression into existence, relatedness and growth, and Herzberg's separation of hygiene factors, whose absence causes dissatisfaction, from motivators, whose presence causes satisfaction - address some of that. Herzberg's distinction is particularly useful at sea: fixing the food and the accommodation removes dissatisfaction but does not by itself motivate anybody.

blocks.h: 4. As Chief Engineer - addressing lack of motivation

blocks.p: Diagnose the level before prescribing the remedy. That is the theory's actual use. Apathy in a motor-man is a symptom; the question is which need is unmet.

ul: Start at the bottom, because it is cheapest and most often the cause. Examine rest hours as they are actually worked, not as recorded; a record that is always exactly compliant is a warning rather than a reassurance. Look at watch patterns, port workload, calls at night, food quality and quantity, cabin air conditioning, hot water, mess and laundry.

Then safety and certainty. Are wages and allotments paid on time; is the contract end date real; has relief been confirmed; is the engine room actually safe to work in. Uncertainty about going home is one of the strongest demotivators at sea and it is not fixed by encouragement.
Then belonging. Include the rating in the daily toolbox talk, use his name, ensure a mixed-nationality crew is not fragmenting at meal times, protect connectivity and recreation time.

Then esteem. Delegate real responsibility with the authority to go with it - give a Fourth Engineer ownership of the purifiers or the boiler and let him report on them. Credit him in front of the department and in the appraisal. Ask before deciding on work he does daily.
Then growth. Plan on-board training, rotate men through unfamiliar machinery, prepare juniors for their next certificate, mentor deliberately rather than incidentally.

Lead by example and be consistent. A Chief Engineer who turns out at 0300 for a blackout, wears the PPE he demands, and applies the same standard to everyone earns the authority that no theory supplies.

blocks.h: 5. As Chief Engineer - addressing differences in attitude

blocks.p: A multinational engine room contains real differences in culture, language, hierarchy-distance, age and expectation, and Maslow is a reminder that people at different levels of need behave differently for reasons that are not defiance. The task is not to erase difference but to prevent it becoming misunderstanding or division.

ul: Set one visible standard for work, safety and behaviour, applied identically regardless of nationality, rank or seniority. Perceived favouritism destroys esteem faster than anything else on this list.

Fix communication first. A working language, briefings confirmed by read-back rather than a nod, written and pictorial checklists, and awareness that in some cultures a junior will not contradict a senior even when he knows the senior is wrong. That is a safety issue as much as a morale one.
Use the structured briefing. Toolbox talks and pre-job briefings give every attitude the same information and the same opportunity to object.

Deal with conflict early, privately and factually; separate the behaviour from the person; and treat bullying, harassment and discrimination as a formal matter, not a personality clash. MLC 2006 and the on-board complaint procedure exist for it.
Mix the teams deliberately on jobs so nationalities and generations work together rather than in blocs, and pair experience with inexperience.
Adjust your own style - direct instruction where a task is safety-critical or time-critical; consultation where the man doing the work knows more about it than you do.

blocks.h: 6. As Chief Engineer - increasing the sense of competitiveness

blocks.p: The stem asks for competitiveness, and the useful reading is constructive competition - measurable improvement against a target and against the department's own past performance - rather than rivalry between individuals, which on a ship damages the teamwork that safety depends on.

ul: Make performance visible and measurable. Fuel and lubricating-oil consumption, specific consumption against the shop trial, boiler and generator running hours, planned-maintenance completion rate, number of overdue jobs, spare-parts stock accuracy, unplanned stoppages. What is measured and displayed improves.
Set targets that belong to the department, not to an individual - a month with no overdue PMS jobs, a reduction in generator running hours in port, a clean unannounced inspection.
Benchmark against the sister ship or the fleet where the company publishes it. Competing with another ship unites the department; competing with each other divides it.

Recognise promptly and specifically. Name the man and the job at the safety meeting; record it in the appraisal; ask the company to recognise it in writing. Recognition delayed to the end of a contract is recognition wasted.
Give ownership of an area - each engineer responsible for named machinery and its performance figures - so the comparison is with the equipment's own history and the pride is in the plant.

Keep it constructive. Never rank men publicly against each other, never let competition encourage short cuts, under-reporting of defects or falsified records, and be alert to competition suppressing the reporting of near misses. A department that competes on how few defects it reports is more dangerous than one that reports many.

blocks.h: 7. The management framework this sits inside

blocks.p: Motivation theory is not the authority for what a Chief Engineer must do; it explains why what he must do works. The obligations come from elsewhere and should be named:

ul: ISM Code - the company must ensure the ship is manned with qualified and medically fit seafarers, provide familiarisation for new personnel, identify training needs, ensure personnel understand the safety management system in a working language, and support the master. Reporting of accidents, near misses and non-conformities, and the master's overriding authority, are the mechanisms by which a well-motivated department actually improves the ship.

STCW 1978 as amended - the Manila amendments introduced competences in leadership, teamworking and managerial skill, at operational and at management level; for a Chief Engineer these are the management-level competences of Table A-III/2, which is why this is examinable at all rather than being merely good practice.

MLC 2006 - the material conditions Maslow's lower levels describe are largely legal entitlements: hours of rest, wages, accommodation and recreational facilities, food and catering, medical care, repatriation, and the on-board complaint procedure. Meeting the MLC is what makes the bottom two levels achievable.

The honest summary. Maslow supplies a diagnostic order; the ISM Code supplies the system; STCW supplies the competence; the MLC supplies the entitlements. A Chief Engineer who uses all four is doing management. One who quotes only the pyramid is doing revision.

blocks.p: Two limbs of very different character under one printed (16). The first is textbook recall - explain Maslow - and almost every candidate will get most of it. The second is a scenario naming three specific issues: lack of motivation, differences in attitude, and increasing a sense of competitiveness. The marks are in the second limb, and they are lost by candidates who spend two pages drawing the pyramid and then write four generic lines about being a good leader. Split the answer roughly one-third to two-thirds, and head the three named issues separately - the examiner listed them, so he is marking them one by one.

The single idea that connects the two limbs is that the hierarchy is a diagnostic tool. Its practical claim is that a satisfied need stops motivating, and that you cannot motivate at a level above the one a person is stuck on. So when the stem says 'lack of motivation', the correct professional response is not a list of encouragements but a question: which level has failed? Praise will not fix exhaustion; a training course will not fix unpaid wages; a bonus will not fix a man who has been on board fourteen months with no relief date. Say that explicitly and the second limb writes itself, because each remedy is then obviously attached to a level.

No convention prescribes a theory of motivation, and Maslow should be attributed as what he is - management and psychological literature, 1943 and 1954. Do not dress it up as an IMO requirement or invent a regulation for it. What is regulatory is the framework around it: the ISM Code on manning, familiarisation and training needs; STCW's leadership, teamworking and managerial competences added by the Manila amendments, at management level for a Chief Engineer; and MLC 2006, which turns most of Maslow's bottom two levels into legal entitlements. Naming those three at the end converts a psychology answer into a Marine Engineering Management answer, which is the function being examined.

blocks.h: Say something about the theory's limits

blocks.p: A short, accurate paragraph on the weaknesses is worth real credit at management level, because it shows judgement rather than recitation. The strict five-level ordering has weak empirical support; the ordering is culturally variable, which matters directly on a multinational ship; the levels overlap rather than queue; and Maslow never drew the pyramid. Herzberg is the most useful supplement for a ship: hygiene factors - food, accommodation, pay, working conditions - cause dissatisfaction when absent but do not motivate when present, whereas motivators - responsibility, recognition, achievement, advancement - do. That is exactly why a ship can have excellent food and a thoroughly demoralised engine room.

ul: Spending most of the answer on the pyramid and treating the scenario limb as an afterthought. The scenario carries the marks.
Not answering the three named issues separately. They are printed as three; mark them as three.
Inventing a regulation for Maslow, or implying the IMO requires the hierarchy. It is management literature.
Giving remedies with no diagnosis - a list of 'motivate the crew, be a good leader' with no link to a level.
Ignoring that competitiveness between individuals can be harmful at sea. Compete against targets, past performance or another ship - not against each other.
Treating 'differences in attitude' as a discipline problem. It is usually culture, language, hierarchy-distance and expectation.
Forgetting that a satisfied need no longer motivates - which is why a pay rise wears off.
Omitting the ISM, STCW and MLC framing, which is what makes this a management-level answer.
Claiming a specific STCW competence wording. Name Table A-III/2; see the uncertainty note below.

blocks.p: "Your Fourth Engineer has stopped caring. What do you do?" Do not answer with encouragement - answer with diagnosis: rest hours as actually worked, food, cabin, pay, relief date, then belonging, then esteem. "You gave him a pay rise and it worked for a month." Exactly what the theory predicts - a satisfied need stops motivating, and pay is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's terms. "Should engineers compete with each other?" Constructive competition against measurable targets, yes; ranking individuals publicly, no - it damages the teamwork safety depends on and encourages under-reporting. "Which regulation requires you to motivate the crew?" None does directly; the ISM Code requires competent, familiarised, supported personnel and the MLC guarantees the conditions - motivation is how you meet those obligations well.

ul: Name Maslow's five levels in order. Physiological, safety, social or belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.
What does prepotency mean? A lower unsatisfied need dominates behaviour until relatively satisfied, and only then does the next level motivate.
Give a shipboard example of each level. Rest and food; a safe engine room and a confirmed relief date; the mess and contact with family; credit and delegated responsibility; promotion and training.
What is the practical use of the theory? Diagnosis - it tells you which remedy will work and which will be wasted.
What are its weaknesses? Weak empirical support for a strict order, cultural variability, overlapping levels; and the pyramid is not Maslow's.
What does Herzberg add? Hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. They are not the same lever.
Where does STCW come into it? The Manila amendments added leadership, teamworking and managerial competences - at management level for a Chief Engineer, Table A-III/2.
Which instrument guarantees the bottom levels? MLC 2006 - hours of rest, wages, accommodation, food, medical care, repatriation.

blocks.p: This question is largely outside the regulatory authority ladder, and that is stated rather than disguised. No instrument prescribes a theory of motivation, so limb one rests on management and psychological literature, attributed to Maslow, Herzberg and Alderfer by name and date. `PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md` §2.1 governs it: the mechanism is explained, the provenance class is declared, and no IMO or statutory rule has been manufactured to satisfy a primary-source checkbox. The Chief Engineer's practical measures in the scenario limb are likewise professional judgement, not requirements.

The regulatory limb is separable and is treated to the higher standard. The ISM, STCW and MLC obligations named above are genuine requirements. One limitation is recorded honestly: MIW does not hold the STCW Code competence tables. The corpus holds the STCW amendment resolutions and supplements, not the base Code. Table A-III/2 is therefore NAMED as the management-level table for engineer officers and NO competence wording is quoted from it. That the Manila amendments introduced leadership, teamworking and managerial competences is carried as verified internal reuse. A session needing the exact wording of a Table A-III/2 competence must obtain the Code.

No figures are given. No percentage improvement in retention, productivity or fuel consumption is claimed for any measure in this answer, because such figures are installation-specific and unverifiable - §2.1 applied, an unverifiable quantity omitted rather than quoted.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q6 on this paper. Q6 asks what MLC Title 1 requires before a seafarer may work at all - old enough, fit enough, trained enough, and recruited through a service that did not exploit him. This question asks what a Chief Engineer does with that person once he is on board. The MLC delivers Maslow's bottom two levels as a matter of law; everything above them is management. Seeing the two questions as the legal floor and the professional ceiling of the same subject is worth more than either answer alone.

A ship in an Indian port is simultaneously Indian territory and foreign territory - subject to India's laws by virtue of where she is, and to her flag State's by virtue of what she is.
