blocks.h: 1. Where India's jurisdiction over a foreign ship comes from

blocks.p: The question contains a trap in its own premise. A foreign ship is under the exclusive jurisdiction of her flag State for the conduct of a safety investigation, so it is worth being precise about why India may inquire at all. The answer is that the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 does not take its jurisdiction here from the flag. Section 358(1) deems a shipping casualty to occur when:

ul: (a) on or near the coasts of India, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded or materially damaged;
(b) on or near the coasts of India, any ship causes loss or material damage to any other ship;
(c) any loss of life ensues by reason of any casualty happening to or on board any ship on or near the coasts of India;
(d) in any place, such a casualty occurs to or on board an Indian ship and a competent witness is found in India;
(e) an Indian ship is lost or supposed lost and evidence is obtainable in India.

blocks.p: Limbs (a), (b) and (c) say "any ship" - they are flag-neutral, and they are the limbs that catch a foreign ship in an Indian port. Only (d) and (e) are confined to Indian ships. India's competence therefore rests on the geography of the casualty, not the nationality of the vessel. Section 357 adds that in this Part "coasts" includes the coasts of creeks and tidal rivers, which brings ports and harbours squarely inside it. Alongside this, India acts internationally as the coastal State (Casualty Investigation Code 2.3) and, where its nationals or interests are engaged, as a substantially interested State.

blocks.h: 2. (i) The machinery of the Merchant Shipping Act

blocks.p: Part XII of the Act is headed Investigations and Inquiries and runs as a sequence:

ol: s.358(2) - notice. The master, pilot, harbour master or other person in charge - of each ship where two are concerned - must give immediate notice of the casualty, on arriving in India, to the officer appointed by the Central Government.

s.359 - preliminary inquiry. On receiving credible information that a shipping casualty has occurred, that officer shall forthwith report in writing to the Central Government, and may proceed to make a preliminary inquiry, sending a report of it to the Central Government. In practice this is the Mercantile Marine Department surveyor acting under the Directorate General of Shipping.

s.360 - application for formal investigation. That officer, whether he has held a preliminary inquiry or not, may apply to a competent court for a formal investigation, and shall do so where the Central Government directs. The court then shall make the investigation.
s.361 - the court. A Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered by the Central Government, or a Metropolitan Magistrate.

s.362 - conduct of individuals. The court may inquire into any charge of incompetency or misconduct against a master, mate or engineer arising in the course of the investigation, and into any wrongful act or default causing the casualty; the person charged must first be furnished with a statement of the case.

s.365 to s.368 - powers. The court has, for compelling attendance of witnesses and production of documents, the same powers as in its criminal jurisdiction; it appoints not less than two and not more than four assessors conversant with maritime or mercantile affairs (s.366); and it may arrest witnesses and enter ships (s.367).

s.369 - the report. The court transmits to the Central Government a full report of its conclusions together with the evidence, and the Central Government causes it to be published in the Official Gazette.
s.370 to s.372 - outcome. Powers to cancel or suspend a certificate granted by the Central Government, to censure a master, mate or engineer, and to remove a master and appoint a new one.

blocks.p: The provision that answers the foreign-ship point directly is s.369(2). Where the investigation affects a master or officer of a ship other than an Indian ship, holding a certificate under the law of a country outside India, the Central Government may transmit a copy of the report together with the evidence to the proper authority in that country. India investigates and reports; the certificate remains the foreign administration's to act on. The same boundary appears in s.363(1)(b): a holder of a foreign certificate may be proceeded against for incompetency or misconduct outside a formal investigation only where it occurred on board an Indian ship.

blocks.h: 3. (i) The international codes that sit above it

ul: Casualty Investigation Code - the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident, resolution MSC.255(84), in force 1 January 2010. Part I general, Part II mandatory standards, Part III recommended practices.

SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, introduced by MSC.257(84), makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory. SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older and broader undertaking to investigate; MARPOL article 12 covers casualties with a major deleterious effect on the environment; UNCLOS article 94(7) sits behind all of them.

The object is prevention, not blame. A marine safety investigation (2.11) is conducted with the objective of preventing marine casualties and marine incidents in the future, and is to be separate from, and independent of, criminal or other investigations. Chapter 11 requires that it not be subject to external direction.

Who investigates. A safety investigation is mandatory into every very serious marine casualty (chapter 6), and the flag State is responsible for ensuring it is conducted. Where India is not the flag State, chapter 7 allows the flag State to agree that another substantially interested State conducts it - and a State conducting or participating in such an investigation discharges its own obligations. Chapters 9 and 10 govern parallel investigations and co-operation.

blocks.p: So the two systems do different work and run side by side. The M.S. Act inquiry is a domestic proceeding which can reach certificates and conduct; the Code investigation is a no-blame safety investigation whose output goes to the IMO. India runs the first over any casualty on its coasts, and takes part in the second as flag State, coastal State or by agreement.

Casualty Investigation Code paragraph 2.9. A marine casualty means an event, or a sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship:

ul: .1 the death of, or serious injury to, a person;
.2 the loss of a person from a ship;
.3 the loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship;
.4 material damage to a ship;
.5 the stranding or disabling of a ship, or the involvement of a ship in a collision;
.6 material damage to marine infrastructure external to a ship, that could seriously endanger the safety of the ship, another ship or an individual;
.7 severe damage to the environment, or the potential for severe damage to the environment, brought about by the damage of a ship or ships.

blocks.p: The exclusion is part of the definition and carries a mark: a marine casualty does not include a deliberate act or omission with the intention to cause harm to the safety of a ship, an individual or the environment. Sabotage and terrorism are therefore not marine casualties, and are dealt with elsewhere. Two neighbouring terms complete the picture: a marine incident (2.10) is an event other than a marine casualty which endangered, or if not corrected would endanger, safety; and a very serious marine casualty (2.22) is a marine casualty involving total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment. Only the last of these triggers a mandatory investigation.

blocks.h: 5. (iii) What the marine safety investigation report consists of

blocks.p: The Code answers this by definition rather than by leaving it to practice. Paragraph 2.12 - a marine safety investigation report means a report that contains:

ol: a summary outlining the basic facts, and stating whether any deaths, injuries or pollution occurred as a result;
the identity of the flag State, owners, operators, the company as identified in the safety management certificate, and the classification society, subject to national privacy laws;
where relevant, the dimensions and engines of any ship involved, with a description of the crew, work routine and other matters such as time served on the ship;
a narrative detailing the circumstances;
analysis and comment on the causal factors, including any mechanical, human and organizational factors;
a discussion of the findings, including identification of safety issues, and the conclusions;
where appropriate, recommendations with a view to preventing future casualties and incidents.

blocks.p: Note what item .5 requires of an engineer's evidence: causal factors are defined at 2.2 as actions, omissions, events or conditions without which the casualty would not have occurred, or its consequences would not have been as serious - and the Code expects organizational factors to be named alongside mechanical and human ones. That is where the ISM Code and the company's own system come under examination.

blocks.h: 6. (iii) How the report reaches the IMO

ol: Draft stage. Under chapter 13 the draft report is sent to substantially interested States for comment, normally allowing 30 days; comments are considered before the report is finalized. Under the recommended practice at 25.2 and 25.3 the same courtesy may be extended to interested parties, again on a 30-day or mutually agreed period.

Submission - the mandatory limb. Chapter 14.1 - the marine safety investigating State shall submit the final version of the report to the Organization for every safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty. Chapter 14.2 - where an investigation into any other casualty or incident produces a report containing information which may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties, that final version shall also be submitted.

The mechanism. Reporting is done electronically into the IMO's Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS), in its Marine Casualties and Incidents module, under the revised harmonized reporting procedures of MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, which implement the reports required by SOLAS regulations I/21 and XI-1/6, MARPOL articles 8 and 12 and Load Lines article 23. Basic factual data is populated as soon as practicable after the occurrence; the full report follows.

Publication. Chapter 14.4 - the final report shall be made available to the public and the shipping industry, or the investigating State shall assist in accessing it where published by another State or the Organization. Domestically, s.369(3) of the M.S. Act requires publication in the Official Gazette.
Disagreement. Paragraph 25.6 - where a substantially interested State disagrees with the whole or part of a final report, it may submit its own report to the Organization.
Use. IMO's III Sub-Committee analyses the reports and the lessons feed back into amendments of the instruments - which is the whole purpose of the no-blame system.

blocks.p: The stem prints (16) on its opening line and then three numbered limbs, so the opening sentence is a heading for the whole question rather than a fourth task - answer the three limbs. They are very unequal in size: (i) is a two-part discursive limb needing both the M.S. Act sections and the international codes; (ii) is a definition; (iii) is content plus a route. Budget accordingly - roughly half the answer on (i), a short (ii), and a full (iii) - and note that (ii) and (iii) are the limbs where exact recall is possible and therefore expected. A definition you can give in the Code's own terms is worth more than a paragraph of approximation.

It asks how the Indian Administration investigates casualties on foreign ships. The instinctive answer - that a foreign ship is the flag State's business - is half right and, given as the whole answer, wrong. The resolution is in the words of section 358(1): limbs (a), (b) and (c) say "any ship", and only limbs (d) and (e) say "Indian ship". India's power over a casualty in its ports is territorial, not flag-based. Then the boundary reappears in the right place: under s.369(2) India may report to the foreign administration but does not touch that administration's certificate, and under s.363(1)(b) it may proceed against a foreign certificate holder outside a formal investigation only where the misconduct occurred on an Indian ship. India investigates the casualty; the flag State disciplines the officer. Getting that division right is what the question is for.

Candidates routinely merge the M.S. Act inquiry and the Casualty Investigation Code investigation into a single process. They are different in purpose, output and consequence. The Act's inquiry is a domestic legal proceeding before a magistrate, with assessors, criminal-jurisdiction powers over witnesses, and outcomes that reach certificates and conduct. The Code's investigation is a no-blame safety investigation, expressly independent of criminal or disciplinary proceedings, whose output is a report to the IMO for the benefit of everyone else. They can run in parallel over the same casualty - chapters 9 and 10 of the Code exist precisely because they do - and the evidence rules differ, which is why chapter 23 protects marine safety records including VDR data from general disclosure. Saying this in two sentences shows the examiner you understand the architecture rather than the vocabulary.

ul: Answering that India has no jurisdiction over a foreign ship. s.358(1)(a)-(c) says "any ship".
Defining very serious marine casualty when the stem asks for marine casualty. They are different paragraphs - 2.22 and 2.9 - and the examiner asked for the wider one.
Omitting the deliberate act exclusion from the 2.9 definition. It is part of the definition.
Inventing report contents for limb (iii). The Code defines them at 2.12, in seven items.
Saying the report goes to IMO 'by letter'. It goes into the GISIS Marine Casualties and Incidents module under MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1.
Saying every casualty report goes to IMO. Mandatory only for a very serious marine casualty (14.1); otherwise only where the report carries information that may prevent future casualties (14.2).
Confusing the preliminary inquiry (s.359, an officer) with the formal investigation (s.360-361, a court). And note s.360 allows an application whether or not a preliminary inquiry was held.
Forgetting the assessors under s.366 - two to four, conversant with maritime or mercantile affairs. It is a favourite oral question.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act 2025. It had assent but had not commenced at this sitting.

blocks.p: "A foreign ship has a fatal engine-room accident alongside in Mumbai. Whose inquiry?" Both. It is a shipping casualty under s.358(1)(c) - loss of life on any ship on or near the coasts of India - so the M.S. Act machinery runs; and it is a very serious marine casualty under the Code, so the flag State must ensure a safety investigation, in which India participates as a substantially interested State or which it conducts by agreement under chapter 7. "Can the Indian court suspend the foreign Chief Engineer's licence?" No - it reports, and under s.369(2) the Central Government may transmit the report and evidence to the issuing authority. "Is a deliberate act a marine casualty?" No, expressly excluded by 2.9. "Who publishes the report?" Internationally, the investigating State must make it public (14.4); domestically, the Official Gazette under s.369(3).

ul: Which Part of the M.S. Act deals with investigations and inquiries? Part XII, sections 357 to 390.
What is a shipping casualty? s.358(1), five limbs - and three of them apply to any ship on or near the coasts of India.
Who holds the preliminary inquiry? The officer appointed by the Central Government under s.358(2), reporting under s.359 - in practice an MMD surveyor under DG Shipping.
Who conducts the formal investigation? A court - a Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Metropolitan Magistrate (s.361).
How many assessors? Not less than two and not more than four (s.366).
Which resolution is the Casualty Investigation Code? MSC.255(84). What makes it mandatory? SOLAS XI-1/6, introduced by MSC.257(84).
Define marine casualty. Code 2.9 - seven limbs, and not a deliberate act intended to cause harm.
What must the report contain? Code 2.12 - summary, identities, ship and crew particulars, narrative, causal analysis, findings and conclusions, recommendations.
When must it go to IMO? Every very serious marine casualty (14.1); and any other report carrying preventive information (14.2).
Through what system? GISIS, the Marine Casualties and Incidents module.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, jurisdiction and the statute in force

blocks.p: The statute in force. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative Indian statute at this sitting and every section cited is a section of it. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received assent on 18 August 2025 but had not commenced; it came into force on 15 March 2026, after this sitting, and it is not relied on anywhere in the model answer. A candidate answering this question at this sitting who cites the 2025 Act is wrong, and the section numbers do not carry across.

What was read, and what was not. The Part XII sections were read in the text of the Act itself, from a copy published on a Government of India domain. MIW does not hold a certified consolidated print incorporating every amendment, so the section numbers and the operative words are relied on; no claim is made about the amendment history of any individual sub-section beyond the amendment footnotes visible in the text read - which show s.361 substituted in 1983 and s.365 renumbered in 1984. The Casualty Investigation Code was read at source in resolution MSC.255(84).

One precision worth recording. GISIS is not mentioned anywhere in the Casualty Investigation Code. The Code says only that the report is submitted to the Organization. The GISIS Marine Casualties and Incidents module and the electronic reporting route come from MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, a separate circular. The two are stated separately above rather than merged, because attributing GISIS to the Code would be a citation error.

Indian administrative practice - that the officer appointed under s.358(2) is in practice a Mercantile Marine Department surveyor acting under the Directorate General of Shipping - is administrative fact rather than statutory text. The Act says only 'the officer appointed in this behalf by the Central Government'. It is stated as practice, and no DG Shipping order or circular number is cited because none is held.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this alongside Q8 on this paper. Both are questions about a foreign ship in an Indian port and the limits of what India may do to her - here the power to inquire into a casualty, there the power to detain for deficiencies. In both the jurisdiction is real but bounded, and in both the boundary is drawn at the same place: India may act on the ship and the facts, but the certificate and the flag State's responsibilities remain the flag State's. Q8 also shares the statute question, since both turn on the 1958 Act having been the law in force on the day.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can India inquire into a casualty on a foreign ship at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because section 358(1) of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 is flag-neutral in its first three limbs. A shipping casualty occurs when, on or near the coasts of India, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded or materially damaged; when any ship causes loss or material damage to another; or when loss of life ensues by reason of a casualty on any ship. Only limbs (d) and (e) are confined to Indian ships. Jurisdiction rests on where the casualty happened, not on the flag.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole question turns on this, and the instinctive answer is the wrong one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a marine casualty.
retrieval_cards.answer: Code 2.9. An event, or sequence of events, resulting in any of the following directly in connection with the operations of a ship: death or serious injury; loss of a person from a ship; loss, presumed loss or abandonment; material damage to a ship; stranding, disabling or collision; material damage to external marine infrastructure endangering safety; or severe damage to the environment, or the potential for it. Excludes a deliberate act intended to cause harm.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (ii) asks for marine casualty, not very serious marine casualty.

A summary of the basic facts stating any deaths, injuries or pollution; the identity of the flag State, owners, operators, the company named in the safety management certificate and the classification society; where relevant the ship's dimensions and engines with a description of the crew, work routine and time served; a narrative of the circumstances; analysis and comment on causal factors including mechanical, human and organizational; discussion of findings, safety issues and conclusions; and recommendations where appropriate.

retrieval_cards.answer: s.358(2) the master gives immediate notice to the officer appointed by the Central Government. s.359 that officer reports forthwith in writing and may hold a preliminary inquiry. s.360 he may, and if directed shall, apply to a court - whether or not a preliminary inquiry was held. s.361 the court is a Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Metropolitan Magistrate. s.366 two to four assessors sit with it. s.369 it reports to the Central Government, which gazettes it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can an Indian court cancel a foreign Chief Engineer's certificate after a casualty in an Indian port?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 369(2) provides that where the investigation affects a master or officer of a ship other than an Indian ship holding a certificate under the law of a country outside India, the Central Government may transmit a copy of the report together with the evidence to the proper authority in that country. India investigates and reports; the issuing administration acts on the certificate. Section 363(1)(b) reaches a foreign certificate holder outside a formal investigation only where the incompetency or misconduct occurred on board an Indian ship.
retrieval_cards.why: This is where the territorial jurisdiction stops, and the examiner will probe it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the M.S. Act inquiry differ from a Casualty Investigation Code investigation?
retrieval_cards.answer: Purpose, output and consequence. The Act's inquiry is a domestic legal proceeding before a magistrate with assessors and criminal-jurisdiction powers over witnesses, and can reach certificates and conduct. The Code's investigation is a no-blame safety investigation, independent of criminal or disciplinary proceedings and not subject to external direction, whose output is a report to the IMO to prevent future casualties. They can run in parallel over the same casualty.
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two is the commonest structural error in this answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instrument makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory, and which parts?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, introduced by resolution MSC.257(84), makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory. The Code itself is resolution MSC.255(84), in force 1 January 2010. Part III is recommended practice. SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older, broader undertaking to investigate, with MARPOL article 12 and UNCLOS article 94(7) behind them.
retrieval_cards.why: Two different resolution numbers doing two different jobs; candidates routinely give only one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does every marine safety investigation report go to the IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Chapter 14.1 makes submission mandatory for every safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty. Chapter 14.2 requires submission for any other casualty or incident only where the report contains information which may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties or incidents. Chapter 14.4 separately requires the final report to be made available to the public and the shipping industry.
retrieval_cards.why: The two limbs of chapter 14 are different obligations and are usually collapsed into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: By what route does the report physically reach the IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: Electronically, into the Global Integrated Shipping Information System, in its Marine Casualties and Incidents module, under the revised harmonized reporting procedures of MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, which implement the reports required under SOLAS regulations I/21 and XI-1/6, MARPOL articles 8 and 12 and Load Lines article 23. Note that GISIS is not named in the Casualty Investigation Code itself.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks how it is relayed, so the mechanism is the answer, not just the obligation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many assessors sit on a formal investigation, and who are they?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 366 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. Not less than two and not more than four, of whom one shall be conversant with maritime affairs and the others with either maritime or mercantile affairs. Where the investigation is likely to involve the cancellation or suspension of a certificate of a master, mate or engineer, two of the assessors must be appropriately qualified persons.
retrieval_cards.why: A standing oral question with an exact numerical answer.

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is built in three parts - the Articles, the Regulations, and the Code. The Code has two halves: Part A Standards, which are mandatory, and Part B Guidelines, which are not, but to which a Member must give due consideration (Article VI). Article VI.3 allows a Member to implement a Part A requirement by substantial equivalence. Title 1 is headed "Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship" and contains exactly the four Regulations this question sets, in this order.

The shape of Title 1 is worth stating before the detail: three of its four Regulations answer the question "may this particular person work at sea at all?" - age, health, competence - and the fourth regulates the system that put them on the ship. That is why recruitment and placement belongs in a Title otherwise about the individual.

blocks.h: 2. (a) Minimum age to work on a ship

blocks.p: Regulation 1.1 - purpose: to ensure that no under-age persons work on a ship. No person below the minimum age shall be employed, engaged or work on a ship. Standard A1.1 sets three separate rules, and the marks are in keeping them apart:

ul: A1.1.1 - the hard floor. The employment, engagement or work on board of any person under the age of 16 is prohibited. There is no exception to this one.

A1.1.2 - night work. Night work of seafarers under 18 is prohibited. Night is defined in accordance with national law, but must cover at least nine hours, starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m.

A1.1.3 - the only exception, and it is to the night rule alone. The competent authority may except a seafarer where effective training under an established programme would otherwise be impaired, or where the specific nature of the duty or a recognized training programme requires night duty and the authority determines, after consultation with shipowners' and seafarers' organizations, that it will not be detrimental to their health or well-being.

A1.1.4 - hazardous work. Employment of seafarers under 18 is prohibited where the work is likely to jeopardize their health or safety. The types of such work are determined by national laws or the competent authority, after tripartite consultation, in accordance with relevant international standards.

blocks.p: So there are two ages, not one: 16 is the absolute minimum for working at all, and 18 is the threshold below which night work and hazardous work are additionally restricted.

blocks.h: 3. (b) Medical certification for duties on board

blocks.p: Regulation 1.2 - seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are certified as medically fit to perform their duties; exceptions only as prescribed in the Code. Standard A1.2 supplies the detail.

ul: Held before starting. A valid medical certificate attesting fitness for the duties they are to carry out at sea must be held prior to beginning work (A1.2.1). The competent authority prescribes the nature of the examination and the certificate after tripartite consultation (A1.2.2).
STCW is accepted. A certificate issued under STCW is accepted for the purposes of Regulation 1.2, so one examination satisfies both instruments (A1.2.3).

Who issues it. A duly qualified medical practitioner, or - for a certificate concerning eyesight alone - a person recognized by the competent authority as qualified. Practitioners must enjoy full professional independence in their medical judgement (A1.2.4). In India this means a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, acting under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it.

Right of further examination. A seafarer refused a certificate, or given a limitation as to time, field of work or trading area, must be given the opportunity of a further examination by another independent practitioner or an independent medical referee (A1.2.5).

What it must state. That hearing and sight are satisfactory - and colour vision where fitness is liable to be affected by defective colour vision; and that the seafarer is not suffering from a condition likely to be aggravated by service at sea, to render him unfit, or to endanger the health of others on board (A1.2.6).

Validity. A maximum of two years; one year if the seafarer is under 18; a certification of colour vision, six years (A1.2.7). These are maxima - a shorter period may be required by the specific duties or under STCW.

Expiry at sea. If validity expires in the course of a voyage, the certificate continues in force until the next port of call where a certificate can be obtained, not exceeding three months (A1.2.9). Separately, in urgent cases, the authority may permit work without a valid certificate to the next port, again not exceeding three months, provided the seafarer holds an expired certificate of recent date (A1.2.8).
Language. For ships ordinarily engaged on international voyages the certificate must be provided as a minimum in English (A1.2.10).

blocks.p: Regulation 1.3 - purpose: to ensure that seafarers are trained or qualified to carry out their duties on board ship. This limb has a feature worth noticing and stating, because it is the one thing here a well-prepared candidate can say that others will not: there is no Standard A1.3 and no Guideline B1.3. Regulation 1.3 stands alone, without a Part A Standard beneath it. The reason is that the detailed requirements already exist elsewhere - in STCW - and the Convention deliberately does not duplicate them.

ul: Reg 1.3.1 - seafarers shall not work on a ship unless they are trained or certified as competent or otherwise qualified to perform their duties.

Reg 1.3.2 - seafarers shall not be permitted to work unless they have successfully completed training for personal safety on board ship. This is the basic safety training limb, and it applies to every seafarer, not only to certificated officers.

Reg 1.3.3 - the bridge to STCW. Training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the IMO shall be considered as meeting the requirements of paragraphs 1 and 2. So an STCW certificate of competency and the STCW basic training discharge this Regulation.

Reg 1.3.4 - a transitional provision preserving obligations under the Certification of Able Seamen Convention, 1946 (No. 74) for Members bound by it, until IMO provisions covering the subject matter enter into force or five years elapse from entry into force of the MLC, whichever is earlier.

blocks.p: Regulation 1.4 - purpose: to ensure that seafarers have access to an efficient and well-regulated seafarer recruitment and placement system. All seafarers shall have access to an efficient, adequate and accountable system for finding employment on board ship without charge to the seafarer. Services operating in a Member's territory must conform to the Code; and a Member must require that shipowners using services based in countries where the Convention does not apply ensure those services conform too (Reg 1.4.3) - the provision that stops the obligation being avoided by recruiting through a non-Party State.

Standard A1.4 regulates the services. A public service must be operated in an orderly manner protecting seafarers' employment rights (A1.4.1). Private services must operate only under a standardized system of licensing or certification or other regulation, established after consultation with shipowners' and seafarers' organizations; and undue proliferation of private services shall not be encouraged (A1.4.2). A Member adopting such a system must at a minimum (A1.4.5):

ul: Prohibit blacklisting - the use of means, mechanisms or lists intended to prevent or deter seafarers from gaining employment for which they are qualified.

Prohibit fees. No fees or other charges for recruitment, placement or providing employment may be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by the seafarer - other than the cost of a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book, and a passport or similar travel document. The cost of visas is expressly excluded and is borne by the shipowner.
Require services to maintain an up-to-date register of all seafarers recruited or placed, available for inspection by the competent authority.
Require that seafarers are informed of their rights and duties before or during engagement, can examine their employment agreements before and after signing, and receive a copy.
Require services to verify that seafarers are qualified and hold the necessary documents, and that agreements accord with applicable law and any collective bargaining agreement.
Require services to make sure, as far as practicable, that the shipowner has the means to protect seafarers from being stranded in a foreign port.
Require services to examine and respond to complaints and advise the competent authority of any unresolved complaint.

Require a system of protection - insurance or an equivalent measure - to compensate seafarers for monetary loss arising from the failure of the service, or of the shipowner under the employment agreement, to meet its obligations.

blocks.p: The competent authority must closely supervise and control all such services, granting or renewing licences only after verification of compliance (A1.4.6), and must ensure machinery exists for investigating complaints about their activities (A1.4.7).

blocks.h: 6. How Title 1 is certified and enforced

blocks.p: Title 1 is not merely aspirational: its four subjects are the first four of the sixteen areas listed in Appendix A5-I which must be inspected and approved before a Maritime Labour Certificate is issued, and they are declared in the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance - Part I stating the national requirements and Part II the shipowner's measures. The certificate and DMLC are accepted by a port State as prima facie evidence of compliance (Reg 5.2.1), and the same subjects appear in Appendix A5-III as areas open to a more detailed port State inspection. On board, the practical evidence a Chief Engineer should expect to be asked for is the age and medical certificate of every engine-room rating, the STCW certificates and basic safety training of the watchkeepers, and the manning agent's licence behind the crew list.

"Write a short note on the following" with four lettered limbs is an instruction about layout as much as content. Four headings, in the printed order, lettered as printed. Roughly four marks each, so roughly equal length - and the commonest failure is to write three pages on medical certificates, because that is the limb most familiar from daily practice, and two lines on recruitment and placement. Resist it. A short framing paragraph naming Title 1 and the mandatory status of Part A is worth having, because it lets all four limbs cite Standards without re-explaining what a Standard is.

blocks.h: The idea that ties the four together

blocks.p: Title 1 answers one question in four ways: who is allowed on the ship in the first place. Age, health and competence are three tests applied to the individual - is this person old enough, fit enough, trained enough. Recruitment and placement is a test applied to the system that supplied them. The Convention's insight is that the first three are worth little if the fourth is unregulated: a manning agent that charges fees, blacklists complainers and cannot be inspected will produce crews who are nominally compliant and actually coerced. Saying that in one sentence turns four disconnected notes into an answer.

blocks.h: The detail that separates a good answer here

blocks.p: There is no Standard A1.3. Regulations 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4 each have a Part A Standard beneath them; Regulation 1.3 does not, and neither does it have a Part B Guideline. That is not an oversight - the Convention points at STCW instead, and Regulation 1.3, paragraph 3 says expressly that training and certification under the IMO's mandatory instruments shall be considered as meeting the requirement. Most candidates will invent a Standard A1.3 to keep the pattern tidy. Stating correctly that none exists, and explaining why, is worth more than a paragraph of invented content - and it demonstrates the candidate has read the instrument rather than a summary of it.

blocks.h: The two ages, and why examiners like them

blocks.p: 16 and 18 do different work. 16 is a prohibition on working at all, with no exception anywhere in the Standard. 18 is a threshold for two further restrictions - night work and hazardous work - and the night restriction is the only one carrying an exception, for training. Candidates routinely merge these into a single vague statement that "young seafarers are protected", or attach the training exception to the age-16 rule, where it does not belong. Set them out as three separate rules and the limb is secure.

ul: Inventing a Standard A1.3. It does not exist. Regulation 1.3 stands alone and points to STCW.
Saying the minimum age is 18. It is 16; 18 is the threshold for night work and hazardous work.
Attaching the training exception to the minimum age. It applies only to the night-work restriction.
Giving medical certificate validity as two years without the qualifications - one year under 18, six years for colour vision, and all of them maxima.

Confusing the two three-month provisions: A1.2.9 is a certificate expiring during a voyage, which continues in force; A1.2.8 is an urgent case where the authority permits work on a recently expired certificate. Different triggers, same ceiling.
Saying the seafarer pays nothing at all. The seafarer may bear the cost of the statutory medical certificate, the seafarer's book and a passport - but not visas, which fall on the shipowner.
Omitting Regulation 1.4.3, the provision reaching services based in non-Party States. It is the limb that makes the rest enforceable.
Forgetting the insurance or equivalent requirement in A1.4.5 - the financial protection against a manning agent's or shipowner's default.
Writing about hours of rest, wages or accommodation. Those are Titles 2 and 3 and earn nothing here.

blocks.p: "What is Standard A1.3?" - a trap question. There is none; Regulation 1.3 has no Part A Standard, and the requirement is met through STCW. "A cadet of 17 is on the 12-4 watch. Any problem?" Yes - night work under 18 is prohibited, and the watch spans the protected period; it is lawful only under the A1.1.3 training exception, granted by the competent authority after tripartite consultation. "His medical expired yesterday, mid-ocean. Must we divert?" No - A1.2.9 continues it in force to the next port of call where a certificate can be obtained, up to three months. "The manning agent deducted one month's wages as a placement fee." Prohibited outright by A1.4.5(b), directly or indirectly, in whole or in part. "Who pays for the visa?" The shipowner - the exclusion is express.

ul: Which Title of the MLC deals with minimum requirements? Title 1, and its four Regulations are 1.1 to 1.4.
Is Part B mandatory? No - Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B Guidelines must be given due consideration (Article VI).
What is substantial equivalence? Article VI.3 - a Member may implement a Part A requirement differently provided it gives effect to the general object and purpose.
How long is a medical certificate valid? Two years maximum; one year under 18; colour vision six years.
Who may issue one? A duly qualified medical practitioner - or, for eyesight alone, a person recognized by the competent authority. In India, a DG Shipping approved examiner.
What if a seafarer is refused a certificate? A1.2.5 - a further examination by another independent practitioner or an independent medical referee.
Can a manning agent charge you a fee? No. A1.4.5(b), other than the statutory medical certificate, seafarer's book and passport. Not visas.
What protects you if the manning agent goes bust owing you wages? A1.4.5(c)(vi) - a system of protection by insurance or equivalent measure to compensate monetary loss.
Where is Title 1 checked on board? Appendix A5-I, the first four of the sixteen areas, declared in the DMLC and inspected for the Maritime Labour Certificate.

blocks.p: AGE - FIT - TRAINED - SUPPLIED. Age (step 2, Reg 1.1 - 16 and 18). Fit (step 3, Reg 1.2 - two, one, six, and three months). Trained (step 4, Reg 1.3 - no Standard, see STCW). Supplied (step 5, Reg 1.4 - no fees, no blacklists, register, insurance). The first three test the person; the fourth tests the system that sent them.

ul: MLC 2006 Article VI - Regulations and Parts A and B of the Code; Part A mandatory, Part B due consideration; Article VI.3 substantial equivalence.
Regulation 1.1 and Standard A1.1 - minimum age. A1.1.1 under 16 prohibited; A1.1.2 night work under 18; A1.1.3 the training exception; A1.1.4 hazardous work under 18.

Regulation 1.2 and Standard A1.2 - medical certificate. A1.2.1 held before starting; A1.2.3 STCW accepted; A1.2.4 who issues; A1.2.5 further examination; A1.2.6 content; A1.2.7 validity; A1.2.8 urgent cases; A1.2.9 expiry during a voyage; A1.2.10 English.
Regulation 1.3 - training and qualifications. No Standard A1.3 and no Guideline B1.3 exist. Reg 1.3.3 routes to the IMO's mandatory instruments; Reg 1.3.4 the Convention No. 74 transitional.

Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4 - recruitment and placement. Reg 1.4.1 without charge; Reg 1.4.3 services in non-Party States; A1.4.2 licensing of private services; A1.4.5 the minimum content, including (a) blacklists, (b) fees, (c)(i) register, (c)(vi) insurance; A1.4.6 supervision; A1.4.7 complaints.
STCW 1978 as amended - the instrument Regulation 1.3 defers to, including basic safety training.
Appendix A5-I - the sixteen areas for inspection and certification; Appendix A5-III - areas open to port State detailed inspection; Regulation 5.2.1 - certificate and DMLC as prima facie evidence.
India: Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it; Directorate General of Shipping approves medical examiners and licenses recruitment and placement services.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the text in force

blocks.p: The amendment position at this sitting. The operative text is the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 as amended. The 2022 amendments were in force at this sitting, having entered into force in December 2024. The 2025 amendments had been adopted but were NOT in force, and nothing from them appears in this answer. Every provision quoted above is quoted from the Convention text itself.

What is not asserted. The amendments of 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022 have concentrated on Titles 2 to 5 - financial security for abandonment and for shipowners' liability, repatriation, harassment and bullying, personal protective equipment, social connectivity and the certification regime. No claim is made here that Title 1 has never been amended, because MIW's verification of the consolidated text is at Regulation and Standard level for Title 1 rather than a clause-by-clause amendment history. The Title 1 provisions above are stated as they stand in the Convention text and were correct at this sitting; a session needing the amendment history of an individual Title 1 paragraph should establish it from the amendment resolutions rather than from this record.

The Indian layer - that DG Shipping approves medical examiners and licenses recruitment and placement services under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - is carried as verified internal reuse from the QP2511 Q3 record. Note that the 1958 Act is the operative Indian statute at this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had assent but had not commenced, and is not relied on anywhere in this answer.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q1 on this paper. Q1 asks for the certificates issued to a vessel for maintaining health on board, and their validity and extension; this question asks for the certificate the seafarer holds, and its validity and extension. The shapes are deliberately parallel - a maximum period, and a limited extension to reach the next port where the document can be obtained - and the instruments are different: the International Health Regulations for the ship, MLC Standard A1.2 for the seafarer. Six months plus one for the ship; two years plus three months for the seafarer. An examiner who has set both on one paper is testing whether the candidate can tell the ship's paperwork from the crew's.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four Regulations of MLC Title 1.
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 1.1 minimum age; Regulation 1.2 medical certificate; Regulation 1.3 training and qualifications; Regulation 1.4 recruitment and placement. Three test the individual - old enough, fit enough, trained enough - and the fourth regulates the system that supplied them.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed limbs map one-to-one onto the four Regulations, in order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: MLC minimum age - which ages, and what does each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two ages. Under 16, employment, engagement or work on board is prohibited outright with no exception (A1.1.1). Under 18, night work is prohibited, night being at least nine hours starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m. (A1.1.2), and work likely to jeopardize health or safety is prohibited (A1.1.4).
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two ages into one statement is the commonest error on this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the training exception let a 15-year-old work on a ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The exception in A1.1.3 applies only to the night-work restriction for seafarers under 18, where effective training would otherwise be impaired or the duty requires it, and only after the competent authority consults shipowners' and seafarers' organizations. The prohibition on anyone under 16 working at all carries no exception.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates attach the exception to the wrong rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long is a seafarer's medical certificate valid, and what happens if it expires at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18; a certification of colour vision a maximum of six years (A1.2.7). These are maxima and a shorter period may be required by the duties or under STCW. If validity expires in the course of a voyage the certificate continues in force until the next port of call where one can be obtained, not exceeding three months (A1.2.9).
retrieval_cards.why: The qualifications carry the marks; the bare two years does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Standard A1.2 paragraph 8 from paragraph 9.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 9 covers a certificate whose validity expires during a voyage - it continues in force to the next port where a certificate can be obtained, up to three months. Paragraph 8 covers urgent cases where the seafarer is already working without a valid certificate - the competent authority may permit it to the next port, up to three months, provided the seafarer holds an expired certificate of recent date. Different triggers, same three-month ceiling.
retrieval_cards.why: Two provisions with the same number of months and different conditions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Standard A1.3 require?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nothing - there is no Standard A1.3, and no Guideline B1.3 either. Regulation 1.3 stands alone without a Part A Standard. Its paragraph 3 provides that training and certification in accordance with the mandatory instruments adopted by the IMO shall be considered as meeting its requirements, so the detail lives in STCW and the Convention does not duplicate it.
retrieval_cards.why: A trap question that rewards having read the instrument rather than a summary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a seafarer never be charged for, and what may they be charged for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A1.4.5(b). No fees or other charges for recruitment, placement or providing employment may be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by the seafarer. The exceptions are the cost of a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book, and a passport or similar personal travel document. The cost of visas is expressly excluded from the exceptions and is borne by the shipowner.
retrieval_cards.why: The visa point is the detail examiners use to separate recall from reading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What protects a seafarer if the manning agent or shipowner defaults on its obligations?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A1.4.5(c)(vi) requires a system of protection, by way of insurance or an equivalent appropriate measure, to compensate seafarers for monetary loss incurred as a result of the failure of a recruitment and placement service, or of the relevant shipowner under the employment agreement, to meet its obligations to them.
retrieval_cards.why: The financial-protection limb is routinely omitted from limb (d).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does Regulation 1.4 reach a manning agent in a country that has not ratified the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 1.4 paragraph 3. Each Member must require, for seafarers working on ships flying its flag, that shipowners using recruitment and placement services based in countries or territories where the Convention does not apply ensure that those services conform to the requirements of the Code. The obligation is placed on the shipowner rather than on the foreign service.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what stops the Title being avoided by recruiting offshore.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are Part B Guidelines mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Under Article VI the Regulations and Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B Guidelines are not, but Members must give due consideration to implementing their Part A responsibilities in the manner provided in Part B. Article VI.3 additionally allows implementation by substantial equivalence. Port State inspection deals only with the Articles, Regulations and Part A Standards.
retrieval_cards.why: Frames every citation in the answer and is a standing oral question.

quick_revision.recall_15s: On a time charter the owner keeps possession, crew and technical management; the charterer buys time and directs EMPLOYMENT. So his influence on machinery is indirect - speed orders giving prolonged low load and fouling, bunkers he supplies and their cat fines, a trading pattern of manoeuvres and starts, cargo demand for heating and reefers, trading limits forcing fuel changeover, and commercial pressure to defer immobilisation. Two clauses price it: the speed and consumption warranty, and the off-hire clause under which hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery - which is why a history of auxiliary breakdown is a recurring off-hire exposure. Before sailing: establish the true condition from PMS, defect list, alarm logs and conditions of class, look for a SYSTEMIC cause, check fuel, critical spares and familiarisation. Options are sail as-is, sail with a restricted envelope, rectify before departure, defer sailing, or recommend she does not proceed. Actions regardless: written assessment to Company and DPA, defects into the SMS, brief the master, order spares, prove the systems, sample the bunkers, match the maintenance plan to the voyage. The ISM Code gives the master overriding authority.

questions.understand_first: The charterer never touches a valve. That single fact organises the whole answer. On a time charter he has bought the ship's time and the right to say where she goes, what she loads and roughly how fast - and every one of those commercial decisions arrives in the engine room as a technical consequence somebody has to absorb. Slow steaming is a commercial decision that shows up as cold corrosion. A cheap bunker stem is a commercial decision that shows up as catalytic fines in the liners. A tight port rotation is a commercial decision that shows up as starting-air compressors running all night. And because hire stops when the machinery does, the owner and the Chief Engineer actually want the same thing, which is why a written, evidence-based assessment before departure is the most powerful instrument a Chief Engineer has. It is not a complaint - it is the argument that spending money now is cheaper than off-hire later.

blocks.h: 1. What a time charter is, and where the charterer's power comes from

blocks.p: Under a time charter the owner keeps possession, the crew and the technical management of the ship and hires out her earning capacity for a period. The charterer pays hire for time, not for cargo carried, and in return acquires the right to direct the ship's employment. The division is the key to the whole question and standard forms such as NYPE express it in an employment and indemnity clause: the master and crew, though the owner's servants, follow the charterer's orders as to employment of the vessel.

So the charterer commands where she goes, what she carries and, within limits, how fast; the owner remains responsible for seaworthiness, manning, maintenance, class and safe operation. The charterer's influence on machinery is therefore almost always indirect - exercised through commercial instructions whose engineering consequences fall on the Chief Engineer. He never orders a setting on the governor; he orders a speed, a port rotation and a bunker grade, and the machinery lives with the result.

blocks.h: 2. The charterer's influences on propulsion and other machinery

ul: Speed instructions. The most direct influence. Orders to slow steam or to run at an economical speed keep the main engine at prolonged low load, with the familiar consequences - fouling of the turbocharger and economiser, poor combustion and deposits, cold corrosion in the liners, exhaust temperature deviations, soot fires in the economiser and the need for auxiliary blowers. Orders to increase speed to make a laycan load the engine near its maximum continuous rating for extended periods.

Bunkers. Under most time charters the charterer supplies and pays for the fuel, and therefore chooses the supplier and the grade within the specification the charterparty allows. That decides the quality the plant must digest - viscosity, density, catalytic fines, sulphur content, stability and compatibility with what is already on board - and it drives purifier settings, filter loading, fuel-pump and injector wear, and changeover management.

Trading pattern and port rotation. Short passages with frequent port calls mean many manoeuvres, repeated starts and stops, high starting-air demand, more time on auxiliary power and less time at steady sea load. Long ballast legs, waiting at anchor and idle time bring their own problems of layup, standby machinery and lubrication.

Cargo-related demand. The cargo the charterer fixes determines the load on ancillary plant - cargo heating and the steam demand it creates, reefer containers and the electrical load, inert gas, tank cleaning and pumping, ballast exchange or treatment, and on some trades the cargo pumps and turbines as a major consumer.

Trading limits and voyage areas. Ice, tropical seawater temperature, high ambient, sediment-laden or biologically rich water for the ballast water treatment plant, and emission-control areas requiring compliant fuel changeover - all follow from the charterer's employment orders.

Time pressure on maintenance. The commercially valuable ship is the moving one. Pressure to defer immobilisation for overhauls, to shorten port stays and to postpone the withdrawal of a generator or a boiler is real and constant. It is exerted commercially, not by instruction, and it is the influence most likely to cause harm.

Efficiency and emissions performance. The charterer's commercial interest in the ship's rating and reported efficiency now shapes instructions on speed, routing, hull and propeller cleaning and voyage optimisation - a further reason for orders that keep the engine off its design point.

blocks.h: 3. Where the charterer's influence is priced - warranties and off-hire

blocks.p: Two clauses turn the Chief Engineer's plant into money, and he should know both.

ul: The description clause and the speed and consumption warranty. The owner warrants the ship's speed and fuel consumption in stated weather conditions. If she under-performs, the charterer claims the time lost and the fuel over-consumed. This is why accurate noon reports, weather data and consumption figures matter commercially as well as technically, and why a fouled hull, a slipping propeller or a mis-set engine becomes a dispute.

The off-hire clause. This is the one that bites on auxiliary breakdown. In the NYPE form, hire ceases for time lost by, among other things, breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel. The ship stops earning while she is unable to perform. A generator failure at sea that forces a speed reduction, or an immobilisation for repair, therefore converts directly into lost hire for the owner - and, where the charterparty is on a net loss of time basis, into an accounting argument about exactly how much time was lost.

blocks.p: That is the commercial reality behind the second half of this question. A history of unforeseen auxiliary breakdown at sea is not merely a technical nuisance; on a time charter it is a recurring off-hire exposure for the owner and a source of claims, and it is what makes the Chief Engineer's pre-voyage work valuable.

blocks.h: 4. Taking over the ship - establishing her true condition

blocks.p: Nothing useful can be decided before the plant's actual state is known, and a handover is the one moment when asking every question is expected. Prior to the voyage:

ol: Take a proper handover. A written handover from the outgoing Chief Engineer, and specifically his account of each auxiliary failure - what failed, what was done, and whether the cause was ever established.

Read the history rather than the last entry. The planned maintenance system - overdue jobs, jobs closed without work, running hours against overhaul intervals; the defect list and outstanding work orders; alarm and trip logs; the engine-room log for repeated abnormalities; previous superintendent and internal audit reports and any open non-conformities.

Establish the class and statutory position. Survey status, conditions of class or memoranda, overdue or postponed surveys, and the status of any equipment under a continuous survey cycle. A condition of class is a constraint on what may be deferred.

Look for the pattern. Repeated breakdown at sea of auxiliary machinery usually has a systemic cause rather than several coincidental ones - commonly fuel quality and treatment, cooling water chemistry or fouling, lubricating oil condition, electrical protection and load sharing, governor or automation faults, or simply maintenance not actually performed. Test the plant against each rather than repairing the last symptom.

Check the consumables and the fuel actually on board. Bunker delivery notes, retained samples, the latest fuel analysis - catalytic fines above all - the condition and settings of the purifiers, filter differential pressures and the compatibility of any blend.

Check spares and stores against the plant. Identification of critical equipment and the spares to support it is an ISM obligation, not a preference. Verify physical stock against the inventory, look at lead times, and identify the single points of failure with no spare on board.

Check the people. Familiarisation of newly joined engineers, competence for the specific plant, watchkeeping arrangements, and readiness for unmanned machinery space operation including alarm transfer and response times.

Read the charterparty extracts the company holds - the description and speed and consumption clause, the off-hire clause, the bunker specification and the trading limits - so that the technical advice given is framed in the terms that will actually be applied.

blocks.h: 5. The options, and what each one means

blocks.p: Having established the condition, the realistic options range from acceptance to refusal, and the Chief Engineer should present them as a recommendation with consequences rather than as a complaint:

ol: Sail as she is, where the investigation shows the failures were addressed and the cause is understood. Legitimate only if it can be justified on evidence.

Sail with mitigation and a restricted operating envelope - additional condition monitoring, more frequent inspections, redundancy preserved by running an extra generator on critical passages, load limits, avoidance of the conditions that provoked the failure. Record the restriction and tell the master and the company.

Rectify before departure - carry out the outstanding work alongside or at anchorage, with maker's or specialist attendance and, where the defect touches a classed item, class attendance. Ask the company for a superintendent.
Request a deferment of sailing, or of the fixture, until a specific defect is rectified. This is the option candidates avoid naming, and it is a proper one.

Recommend that the vessel not proceed where the plant cannot be made fit for the intended voyage. The master's overriding authority under the ISM Code exists for exactly this, and the Chief Engineer's role is to give him the technical basis for using it.

blocks.h: 6. Actions prior to commencement of the voyage

ul: Put the assessment in writing to the Company and the DPA. A verbal concern is not a record. State the defect, the risk, the option recommended and what is needed - it is also the mechanism by which the ISM system is supposed to work, and it moves the decision to the level that can fund it.
Raise the outstanding items formally in the safety management system as defects or non-conformities so they are tracked rather than remembered.

Brief the master fully, in terms of operational consequence rather than machinery detail - what she can and cannot do, what the plant will not tolerate, and what he should not accept in an employment order.
Order the critical spares and press for delivery before departure; where they cannot arrive in time, say so explicitly in the written assessment.

Test and prove the essential systems before sailing - generators on load and in parallel, automatic start of the standby set, blackout recovery and the emergency generator, steering gear, main engine trials and reversing, the emergency fire pump, bilge and ballast systems, boiler safety devices and alarm transfer.
Sample and analyse the bunkers before use, and do not use a stem of doubtful compatibility on a critical passage while the result is outstanding.

Set the maintenance plan against the actual voyage - schedule immobilisation and heavy work for ports where it is feasible, and agree it with the master and the company in advance so it is not competing with a fixture later.
Bring the crew into it. Brief the engineers on the failure history and the watch response; run drills for blackout and for the specific failure mode seen before.

Keep the commercial and technical roles separate. The Chief Engineer advises on the ship's technical condition; he does not negotiate with the charterer, accept employment orders, or comment on hire and off-hire. Those are the master's and the owner's. Where pressure to sail is applied, record it, refer it to the company, and let the master's overriding authority operate.

blocks.h: 7. The line the Chief Engineer must not let be crossed

blocks.p: A charterer may direct employment. He may not direct unsafe operation, and no charterparty instruction overrides the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy, properly maintained ship or the master's authority to refuse. The ISM Code makes the company responsible for the ship's maintenance and for supporting the master, and gives the master overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention. The practical discipline is simple: let the commercial pressure be answered commercially and the engineering question answered on engineering evidence, and put the engineering answer in writing before the ship sails, not after she breaks down.

Two limbs, and the second is longer than it looks. The first asks for the influences of a charterer on machinery operation - a discussion. The second is a scenario with two explicit demands: state the different option you have and actions you would takes, both prior to the commencement of voyage. That is three things to head, not two, and options and actions are not the same list - options are the courses open to you, actions are what you do regardless of which you choose. Candidates who merge them lose the marks for the one they left out. The words prior to the commencement of voyage also bound the answer: describing how you would fix a generator at sea does not answer this question.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb one coherent

blocks.p: The charterer never touches the machinery. On a time charter the owner keeps possession, crew and technical management; the charterer buys the ship's time and directs her employment. So every influence in limb one is indirect - a commercial instruction with an engineering consequence. He orders a speed, and the Chief Engineer gets prolonged low load, fouling and cold corrosion. He buys the bunkers, and the Chief Engineer gets the catalytic fines. He fixes a short-sea trade, and the Chief Engineer gets manoeuvres and starting-air demand. Saying that once, at the top, turns a shopping list into an argument - and it is also the sentence that sets up limb two, because it explains why the pre-voyage assessment is the Chief Engineer's real point of leverage.

blocks.h: Know the two clauses that convert engineering into money

blocks.p: At management level the examiner expects commercial literacy. Two clauses do the work. The speed and consumption warranty in the description clause exposes the owner to a claim for time lost and fuel over-consumed if the ship under-performs - which is why noon reports and consumption figures are commercially live documents. The off-hire clause is the one that matters for this scenario: hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel. A history of unforeseen auxiliary breakdown at sea is therefore a recurring off-hire exposure, not merely a technical nuisance, and naming that is what shows you understand why the company should fund the repairs you are about to ask for.

blocks.h: Options and actions - keep them apart

blocks.p: Set the options out as a ladder with consequences: sail as she is; sail with mitigation and a restricted operating envelope; rectify before departure with maker's or class attendance; request deferment of sailing; recommend that she not proceed. Name the last two. Candidates instinctively avoid them because they sound like refusing to work, but they are proper professional options and the master's overriding authority under the ISM Code exists precisely so that they can be exercised. Then the actions - written assessment to the Company and DPA, defects raised in the SMS, master briefed, critical spares ordered, systems proved before sailing, bunkers sampled, maintenance plan matched to the voyage, crew briefed and drilled. Those you do whichever option is chosen.

ul: Writing about a voyage charter or a bareboat charter. The stem says time charter, and the division of responsibility is what the question turns on.
Saying the charterer instructs the Chief Engineer on machinery. He does not - he directs employment, and the machinery consequences follow.
Merging options and actions into one list when the stem asks for both.
Answering what you would do at sea when it breaks down. The stem says prior to the commencement of voyage.
Omitting off-hire entirely. It is the clause that makes auxiliary breakdown expensive and it is the commercial hinge of the scenario.
Treating each past breakdown as an isolated event instead of looking for the systemic cause - fuel, cooling, lube oil, electrical protection, automation, or maintenance not actually done.
Forgetting conditions of class and survey status, which constrain what may legitimately be deferred.
Not putting anything in writing. A verbal concern is not a record and does not move the decision to the company.
Straying into the commercial role - negotiating with the charterer, or opining on hire. That is the master's and the owner's ground.
Inventing a regulation that governs charterer's instructions. There is none; the constraints are the charterparty, the ISM Code and the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship.

blocks.p: "The charterer has ordered slow steaming. Can you refuse?" Not as a commercial order - speed is employment. But you advise on the technical consequences, agree load limits and countermeasures, and if prolonged low load would endanger the plant or the ship you say so in writing and the master decides. "The charterer's bunkers are off-specification. Whose problem?" The charterparty allocates it, but the immediate engineering decision is yours - do not burn a doubtful stem on a critical passage while the analysis is outstanding. "The company says sail, you say the generator is unfit." Put the technical assessment in writing to the Company and the DPA and brief the master; the ISM Code gives the master overriding authority. "Is a generator breakdown off-hire?" Under a typical NYPE off-hire clause, time lost by breakdown of machinery preventing the full working of the vessel is - but it is the master's and owner's ground to argue, not yours.

ul: What does a time charterer actually control? Employment - where she goes, what she carries, and within limits how fast. Not possession, crew or technical management.
Who buys the bunkers on a time charter? Normally the charterer, within the specification the charterparty allows.
What is off-hire? A clause under which hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel.
What is the speed and consumption warranty? The owner's warranted performance in stated weather; under-performance exposes him to a claim for time lost and fuel over-consumed.

Give three machinery consequences of prolonged slow steaming. Turbocharger and economiser fouling, poor combustion and deposits, cold corrosion of liners; also auxiliary blower running and soot fires.

What would you look at first on taking over a ship with a breakdown history? The PMS - overdue jobs, jobs closed without work, running hours against overhaul intervals - then the defect list, alarm and trip logs, and conditions of class.
What is a condition of class? A requirement imposed by the society to be completed by a stated date; it constrains what can be deferred.
Which spares must be on board? Those supporting identified critical equipment, under the ISM Code.
Who can refuse to sail? The master, under his overriding authority in the ISM Code. The Chief Engineer supplies the technical basis.

blocks.p: For limb one, S - B - T - C - L - M: Speed, Bunkers, Trading pattern, Cargo demand, Limits and areas, Maintenance pressure (step 2), then the two clauses that price it (step 3). For limb two, FIND - CHOOSE - DO: find the true condition (step 4), choose among the options (step 5), and do the actions regardless of the choice (step 6).

ul: ISM Code - the company's responsibility for maintenance of the ship and equipment; identification of critical equipment and systems whose sudden failure may result in a hazardous situation, with measures to promote reliability; familiarisation of newly joined personnel; reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; and the master's overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention. This is the regulatory limb of the answer.
SOLAS chapter IX - the mandatory basis of the ISM Code.
Classification society rules - survey status, conditions of class and memoranda; continuous survey cycles. Class technical material, not an IMO instrument.

NYPE and similar time-charter forms - the employment and indemnity clause, the description and speed and consumption warranty, the off-hire clause, the bunker specification and trading limits. Commercial contract practice, not regulation - see the uncertainty note.
ISO 8217 - the marine fuel specification a charterparty bunker clause normally references. Named; MIW holds no licensed copy and no clause of it is quoted.
MARPOL Annex VI - the sulphur limits and emission control areas behind compliant-fuel changeover, named as the reason a trading area drives a fuel decision.

blocks.p: Most of this question has no regulatory source, and that is stated rather than disguised. No instrument governs what a charterer may instruct - the constraints are the charterparty, which is a commercial contract between owner and charterer, the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship, and the ISM Code. `PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md` §2.1 governs the charterparty and engineering limbs: the mechanisms are explained, the provenance class is declared, and no regulation has been manufactured to govern charterer's instructions.

Charterparty terms are described generically and by function. NYPE and the other standard forms exist in several editions with materially different wording, and their terms are amended by rider clauses in every fixture. No clause number is cited and no charterparty wording is quoted; the employment clause, the speed and consumption warranty and the off-hire clause are described by what they do. Whether a particular breakdown puts a particular ship off hire depends on the actual wording of the actual fixture - including whether it operates on a net-loss-of-time or a period basis - and the answer says so rather than asserting an outcome.

The regulatory limb is separable and is treated to the higher standard. The ISM Code obligations - maintenance of the ship and equipment, identification of critical equipment, familiarisation, reporting, and the master's overriding authority - are genuine requirements and are the ones the answer relies on when it says the Chief Engineer's route is a written assessment to the Company and the DPA.

No figures are quoted. No percentage of fuel saved by slow steaming, no consumption figure, no interval for any overhaul and no threshold for catalytic fines is asserted, because all of them are engine, maker and installation specific. The mechanisms are described and the parameters named - §2.1 applied, an unverifiable quantity omitted rather than given false precision.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q8 on this paper. Both ask what happens when a ship is not fit to do what she is being asked to do - here the pressure is commercial and the safeguard is the master's overriding authority and a written assessment; there the pressure is regulatory and the safeguard is a port State detention. The two questions approach the same defect from opposite directions, and the same discipline answers both: establish the condition on evidence, record it in writing, and do not let the decision be made by whoever is in the greatest hurry.

questions.understand_first: Two legal systems meet on one ship, and the whole question is about keeping them apart. Section 334 is Indian domestic law: it describes a state, and its consequence is a criminal offence after the fact. Port State control is international law borrowed by any port State from the conventions: it describes an intervention, and its consequence is that the ship does not move. A ship can be detained abroad without anyone in India being prosecuted, and prosecuted under s.334 without ever having been detained. Once that is clear, the third limb stops being a list to memorise and becomes obvious - the procedure exists to get a ship that cannot be made safe alongside to a place where she can, without pretending she is safe in the meantime.
